en: The vessels for the men were provided by King Kuntibhoja, the father of Kuraṅgī;
[he was] a Kauñjāyana.
Bhūtika—two ministers of Kuntibhoja.
Bhaṭa—the doorkeeper of Kuntibhoja named Jayasena.
Avimāraka—the son of the King of Sauvīra.
Vidūṣaka: A friend of Avimāraka named Santuṣṭa.
Sauvīrarāja: The father of Avimāraka.
Nārada: A celestial sage (devarṣi).
The Vidyādhara is the giver of the ring to Avimāraka. The female roles are played by the queen, the consort of Kuntibhoja.
Kuraṅgī—the daughter of Kuntibhoja;
Sudarśanā—the mother of Avimāraka and queen of the King of Kāśī;
the female doorkeeper—the gatekeeper of Kuntibhoja.
Maid: Kuraṅgī’s servant is named Candrikā.
Nurse: Kuraṅgī’s foster-mother is named Jayadā.
Nalinikā: [She is] Nalinikā.
Māgadhikā: She is the attendant of Kuraṅgī;
she is the courtesan Vasumitrā.
Hariṇikā and Saudāminī— the beloveds of the Vidyādhara—
and the two attendants of the Queen.
Act One.
(At the conclusion of the *nāndī*, the Stage Manager enters.

Stage Manager: [She who was] lifted with compassion from the waters of the ocean, resting upon the tip of a single tusk; who was overcome in the midst of battle and whose sons of Diti were slain; and who was cast down by the strike of a single foot—[this Earth...]

May the glorious Nārāyaṇa bestow upon you the earth, enjoyed with affection, brought under the control of your own arm, protected by the single umbrella of sovereignty, and shaded by the uplifted single parasol. || 1 ||
(Looking toward the tiring-room) Noble lady! This way, please. Actress: Noble sir! Here I am.
Director: Noble lady! Your inner feeling has been revealed, as it were, by your smile born of curiosity regarding my face. Surely you wish to say something?
Actress: What is there to wonder at? The noble sir is one who understands the inner state of others. Director: In that case, speak freely.
Actress: I wish to go to the garden with the noble sir; for I have a woman’s duty, a religious observance (*niyama*), to perform there.
(That which is to be done by a woman is a matter of restraint.
(Behind the scenes:
Bhūtika! You too must go to the garden for the sake of guarding Kuraṅgī; for Añjanagiri is under my control.
Director: Noble lady, have you not heard that the princess has gone to the garden?
Therefore, at present, the gardens are guarded on all sides. Once the princess has returned, we shall go as we please.
Actress: As the noble sir commands.
(They both exit. End of the prologue. (Then the King enters with his retinue.)
King: Sacrifices have been performed, the best of the twice-born are pleased with me, and the lords of men, intoxicated by their power, have been made to taste the flavor of fear;
yet, despite this, my mind finds no joy.
For a father of a daughter, indeed, there is always much to be contemplated. || 2 ||
Ketumatī! Go and bring the Queen.
Portress: As the Master commands. (Exit.
(Then enters the Queen with her retinue.)
Queen: Victory to the Great King! King:

Queen, although your face is ever serene, today it seems exceptionally radiant. What is the cause of this great joy? Queen: Indeed, the Great King has said that a messenger has arrived on account of Kuraṅgī; therefore, I shall soon behold my son-in-law. (The Great King has indeed said...)
"A messenger has arrived, saying: 'Behold your son-in-law before long. The King: "Such a thing indeed exists, yet no final decision has been made. Come, sit down.
The Queen: "As the Great King commands."
(He sits down.
King: O Queen, marriages must indeed be performed after repeated examination. Why?
Because one should not enter into a marriage without considering the excellence of the son-in-law.
But she was given by her father according to his own desire;
for a woman, through intoxication, destroys both families, just as a river with agitated waters destroys its two banks. (3)
Ah, it is like a sound! There must be many causes for this;
for he, due to his great size, appears as if nearby even though he stands at a distance.
Despite thousands of reasons [for caution], my mind suspects the female deer. (4)
Queen: Ah! My daughter has gone to the garden.
King: Who is here? (Enter)
Soldier: Victory to the Great King! Here is the noble Kauñjāyana, arrived to report.
King: Let him be admitted at once. Soldier: As the Great King commands. (Exit.)
(Then enters Kauñjāyana.

Kauñjāyana—(With despondency) Alas! What misery is this so-called office of a minister! For why? When affairs are successful, people proclaim the power of the king; but when they fail, they speak of the minister’s lack of ability.
In times of misfortune, it makes the faults of the ministers' counsel clearly manifest.
These wicked men, though called "ministers" by kings with words that are pleasing to the ear and noble, are punished most subtly, even though they are experts in the art of intellect and counsel.

Jayasena! In which part of the palace is my lord? What do you say? "In the audience hall. Therefore, this ground is not to be feared. (Walking about with agitation) May my lord be gracious! King: Enough, enough of this agitation! Sit down at ease and tell me what has happened.
Kauñjāyana: Let my lord listen. Was I not told by my lord, "Go to the garden with the lady"?
The King: It was so said. What more?

Kauñjāyana: Then, after the princess had returned from sporting at her pleasure in the garden, an elephant arrived at that place, blinded by rut. Its face was clouded by the downpour of ichor flowing from its temples, which was intensified by the laughter and talk of the male and female servants. Having struck down and killed several riders, it was covered with the dust of the earth, its terrifying form only faintly visible. Like the wind incarnate, moving swiftly through both seen and unseen spaces, as if desiring to provoke reproach among the king’s ministers, or wishing to reveal some particular individual, the elephant approached that spot, intoxicated with passion.
The King: Let the details suffice. Is not Kuraṅgī well?
Kauñjāyana: How could she be unwell while her master’s fortunes remain intact? The King: By good fortune! You may now speak as you please.

Kauñjāyana: Then, while the common folk were fleeing, while the women could offer no remedy other than cries of "Alas!", while the noble men had taken refuge [in hiding], and while I, Nītigupta, was momentarily distracted by the inspection of all the equipment in the garden, that elephant suddenly reached the very carriage of the princess. Queen: Oh! What indeed will happen hereafter? King: Then by whom was the doe protected?
Kauñjāyana: Now, there was a certain man who was handsome—(he stops after saying this much).
The King: Speak now as you wish; calamities cannot be avoided.

Kauñjāyana: Now, there was a certain man who, though handsome, was free from pride; though young, he was devoid of arrogance; though brave, he was courteous; though delicate, he was strong—in [his devotion to] the lady of our master...

While she was being overwhelmed by the elephant, he fearlessly approached that noble beast, having granted her a safety so difficult to obtain at such a time. The King: He has discharged his debt of compassion. And then? Kauñjāyana: Then, provoked by the master’s playful yet impetuous striking with his palm, that rogue elephant suddenly abandoned the lady of the house and turned back, intent on killing him alone.
Queen: May it be well with you.

Kauñjāyana: Immediately thereafter, Bhūtika arrived, and together with me, we placed the princess back upon the carriage, brought her quickly, and entered her into the inner apartments of the maidens.
King: Oh, what a great negligence! Now, for what reason did Bhūtika not come?

Kauñjāyana: I was told by Bhūtīka, "Go and report this matter to my master; once I have ascertained that man's conduct and lineage, I shall return quickly. The King: In that case, Bhūtīka will return after having investigated everything. Kauñjāyana: My Lord, he deceives himself here, saying, "I am an outcaste. The King: Kauñjāyana, from which family is this helper in another's distress descended?
Kauñjāyana: My Lord, he says here, "I am an outcaste," thus deceiving himself.
Queen: O Great King! How could one who is of low birth be so compassionate?
King: What indeed could this be?
(Then Bhūtika enters.)

Bhūtika—(With astonishment) Oh, how the earth conceals its jewels! Indeed, by the unfeigned prowess of this man, the martial ambitions of the high-minded seem to have been dampened. Yet I have one doubt: for what purpose does he conceal his identity and his lineage? Or rather, who is capable of covering the sun with his hand? For in this world, virtuous men remain hidden on earth by some means or other.

Though restrained by their own reasons and by their elders, they repeatedly encounter the calamities of others; desiring to escape them, they forget their previous restraint and turn back toward vice.

Jayasena! In which part of the palace is my lord? What do you say? "In the audience hall. Therefore, this ground is free from suspicion; I shall enter. (Entering) Ah, here is the Great King seated with the Queen. (Approaching) Victory to the Great King! King: Queen, enter the inner apartments and comfort Kuraṅgī. I too shall follow immediately after you.
Queen: As the Great King commands.
(Exit.
King: What news is there of him, who disregarded his own body for the sake of another?

Bhūtika: Let my lord listen. Having played for a moment with that elephant—without disdain, without haste, and with grace as if with a dear friend—and having bewildered it with various maneuvers of turning back, following after, and changing its course, the elephant, as if ashamed by that performance and unable to endure the praise of the great multitude, went slowly to his own quarters with his head bowed low.
The King: Oh, I am pleased! For this is my second gain.

Bhūtika: Immediately thereafter, having perceived that excellent elephant, I had him seized by female elephants, brought into this elephant stable, and then I departed under some pretext to ascertain the man's activities and lineage.
The King: What then? What decision was made? We have heard that he is an outcaste.
Bhūtika: What is there to examine here?
His form is divine, born of Brahman; his speech is that of a Kṣatriya, as are his splendor, delicacy, and strength.
If this were so, his status as an outcaste would indeed be true, and our exertion in the paths of the scriptures would be in vain. (7)
The King: Does he have a wife?
Bhūtika: He has everything; however, as for a wife, he has not yet married. The King: Even though the sight of women has been avoided by him, why was his father not examined?
Bhūtika: Your Majesty has been seen; you are blessed with a worthy son.
For he—whose broad, high, and long shoulders are firm from physical exercise, and whose forearms are prominent with calluses formed by the striking of bowstrings—...
Though concealed, his royal nature is recognizable by its imitation [of kingly traits], like the sun within a cloud, to be inferred from its radiance. || 8 ||
The King: Enough with this digression. Let this matter be examined once more.
Bhūtika: As my lord commands. The King: Now, what should be done regarding the messenger from the King of Kāśī?
Bhūtika said: "O Master! Hundreds of messengers have arrived and more are yet to come.
There is nothing further to be done there; in this world, the status of being a father of a daughter is highly venerable."
For all the lords of men, like wrestlers, vie for the daughter of the king as if for a banner. || 9 ||
The King: What is your intention?

Bhūtika: One should not show courtesy in every situation. The meaning is that, having considered the abundance of virtues as well as the immediate and future consequences, one should abandon both haste and procrastination and accomplish the task without violating the requirements of place and time. The King: Bhūtika has spoken rightly. Kauñjāyana! Why have you become silent?

Kauñjāyana said: "O Lord! Among many Kṣatriyas, the King of Sauvīra and the King of Kāśi—due to their specific prior connections as the husbands of Your Lordship’s sisters—are equal in their fitness for our alliance; thus they were considered by Your Lordship. In that regard, the King of Sauvīra previously dispatched a messenger on account of his son. We dismissed him with great honor, using the pretext that the girl was still very young. Now, however, the King of Kāśi has dispatched a messenger on account of his son. In this matter of weighing the relative strength of the two cases, Your Lordship is the authority."

The King: Kauñjāyana has spoken rightly. Bhūtika! When all the circle of kings has been set aside and only two remain, which one do you prefer? Bhūtika: Kings are not to be faulted by their servants; for sovereignty belongs to the masters over their ministers.
The King: Enough of this formal courtesy. Speak plainly; what is your decision?

Bhūtika: But now, it must not be rejected. My lord! The King of Sauvīra and the King of Kāśi are equal in their relation as husbands of your sister. However, because he is the brother of the Queen, the Lord of Sauvīra is superior in merit.
King: Indeed, you do not follow my own intention.
Bhūtika: I am favored in both ways.
King: Ho there! Why indeed has the lord of Sauvīra not sent an envoy again?
Bhūtika: I have some doubt regarding that matter; I did not say that I would speak only after having investigated it thoroughly.
The King: But is His Honor doing well?
Bhūtika: The scouts report that His Honor is not to be seen with his son; it is said that the ministers are conducting the affairs of state.
There is no cause for this whatsoever; entry into the royal palace is not permitted. || 10 ||
The King: Oh, what indeed could this be?
Is he struck by passion, or has he been seized by evil-minded ministers, or is he looking upon his own people while afflicted by disease?
Having been cursed by the twice-born, he observes a vow and performs penance;
what indeed could be the cause for the king’s confinement in his own palace? || 11 ||
"Let this matter be investigated immediately. Bhūtika: "As my lord commands.
The King: "Kauñjāyana! What should now be done regarding the messenger from the King of Kāśi?"
Kauñjāyana: Under these circumstances, the messenger from the King of Kāśī must be honored. Marriages have many facets and can be accomplished according to one's desire.
The King: Alas! The intellect of ministers considers only the task at hand, not affection.
(Offstage)
Victory to the Master! Victory to the Great King! Ten *nālikās* have been completed.
Bhūtika: "Master! We shall consider the remainder within. The time for the bath is passing; the Master’s daughter must be comforted, and the Queen Mother has waited for a long time.
Furthermore, the great populace, amidst this disturbance, desires to see the Master."
The King: Alas, what a great burden is this thing called sovereignty! Why so?

Dharma must be considered first; the course of the ministers' intellects must be scrutinized with one's own wisdom; passion and anger must be concealed; and the qualities of mildness and severity must be employed according to the requirements of the time.
One should observe the circle [of the enemy] by means of the spies and scouts acting as eyes, following worldly custom;
yet, while one's own self must be protected with effort here at the head of the battle, that [enemy] should not be looked upon again. || 12 ||
(All exit. End of the First Act.
The Second Act begins.
(Then enters the Vidūṣaka.

Vidūṣaka: Oh! Sons of nobles truly do not understand the distinctions of circumstances. Therefore, since His Highness Avimāraka saw Kuraṅgī—the daughter of Kuntibhoja—on the day of the elephant-panic, he has become as if transformed from that moment on. Alas, alas! What more need be said? He does not even wish to go to the cow-pen with me; he remains absorbed, thinking only of her.

Truly, the worldly saying that "those who wander for alms bring misfortune" is false. What connection is there here? The daughter of a courtesan is herself of low birth. As for me, avoiding the censure of Brahmins, I shall wander among the families of Brahmins and then go secretly to the very residence of His Honor. (O! Those called the sons of lords do not understand the particularities of circumstances.)

Therefore, the venerable Avimāraka—disregarding the ruin of his lineage through a sage’s curse, his own exile to the family of an outcaste, and even his elders—has become as if transformed ever since he beheld Kuraṅgī, the daughter of Kuntibhoja, on the day of the elephant-panic. Alas, alas! What need is there for much? He does not even wish for conversation with me; he delights only in constant brooding. Truly, the popular proverb is right: "Misfortunes come in pairs."

What connection is there here? That princess herself is an outcaste! For my part, avoiding any censure of the Brahmins, I shall wander among the families of Brahmins and, remaining incognito, go directly to the residence of His Highness. (Then enters a maidservant.)

Maid: Since the King has departed from this state [of distress], I have come out to see the city as there is little to do [here]. (Walking about and looking) Ah, here goes the noble Santuṣṭa. Very well; I shall divert my weariness for a moment by joking with him. (Approaching and looking up) Friend Komudikā! Have you found the Brahmin? What...?

"You say, 'I cannot find him. (While the royal household is thus distracted by this situation, she has gone out to look at the city because there is not much business here. Oh! Here goes the noble Santuṣṭa. Well then, I shall dispel my boredom for a moment by joking with him. "Friend! Kaumudikā! Have you found the Brahmin? "What do you say? 'I have not found him'? Vidūṣaka: "Candrikā! What is this? Maid: "Noble sir! I am searching for a certain Brahmin."
Vidūṣaka: What business does a brāhmaṇa have?
Maid: What else? To invite him for a meal.
Vidūṣaka: Madam! Who am I? A mere ascetic!
Maid: You, it is said, are ignorant of the Vedas (*avaidika*).
Vidūṣaka: Why am I ignorant of the Vedas? Listen for a moment. There is a treatise on dramaturgy called the *Rāmāyaṇa*. Five verses from it were read by me within less than a year.
Maid: I know, I know! Such a manifestation of intelligence is worthy of your noble lineage. Vidūṣaka:
Not only the verses, but their meaning as well has been understood. Moreover, there is another distinction: a Brāhmaṇa who knows both the letters and the meaning is rare to find.

Maid: Then tell me, what is this syllable? (She shows the name-seal. Vidūṣaka: (To himself) Not knowing it, what shall I say? (Reflecting) Very well, I have seen it. I shall speak thus. (Aloud) Lady! This syllable is not in my book. (Not knowing it, what shall I say? Very well, I have seen it. I shall speak thus. Lady! This syllable is not in my book.)
Maid: If you do not know, then eat without offering the ritual gift.
Vidūṣaka: Enough, enough! Maid:
Let me first look at the noble sir’s ring.
Vidūṣaka: Look, look! Behold my handsome appearance! Maid:
(Taking him by the hand) Here comes the young master from this very direction!
Vidūṣaka: (Turning around and looking) Where, where is His Honor?

Maid: The simple Brahmin has been enticed. Having entered this crowd of people, I shall deceive him at the crossroads and depart. (Exit. (The simple Brahmin has been enticed. Having entered this crowd of people, I shall deceive him at the crossroads and go.)

Vidūṣaka:—(Looking all around) Candrikā! Candrikā! Where, where is Candrikā? Alas, I have been deceived! Even though I knew the character of this slave-girl Gaṇḍabheda, I was betrayed by my own misplaced confidence in her. (Walking about) I even suspect that the food was false. (Looking ahead) Ah, here she runs! Stop, stop, you most wicked slave-girl! Stop! Why do you just keep running? I shall run after you too!

(He runs. My feet stumble here and there, as if I were being attacked by an elephant in a dream. Alas! I shall inform my lord of the Kumbhadāsī’s conduct. (Candrikā! Candrikā! Where is Candrikā? Where is she? Ah, I am deceived! Though I knew the character of the slave-girl Gaṇḍabheda, I was betrayed by the confidence she placed in me regarding food. I even suspect that the food itself was false. Alas! She is running away! Stop, stop, you most unrighteous slave-girl! Stop!
Why is he running? I shall run as well. My feet fall here and there, as if I were being struck by an elephant in a dream. Alas! I shall report the news of Kumbhadāsī to your honor. (Exit. Interlude.
(Then enters Avimāraka, seated.
Avimāraka: Even now, I recall that young woman whose limbs were cooled by the spray from an elephant's trunk, her eyes trembling and despondent with fear.
Having constantly perceived [this] in dreams, I now remember it upon waking, as one who remembers their former birth recalls their very first birth. || 1 ||
Oh, the power of the bodiless god! Why?
Because from that moment on, her gaze no longer desires any other form;
her intellect exults and yet languishes as she remembers him.
My face turns pale, my body grows thin, and I fall into grief by day and into delusion by night. || 2 ||

Or rather, it is improper for men to lack self-control; for passion expands with the mind’s intention. Therefore, I shall not form such an intention now. (Recalling) Oh, the perfection of her beauty! Her youth is commensurate with her beauty, and her delicacy is worthy of her youth. For here, has the Creator fashioned this as a prototype for the forms of young women?

Or has Lakṣmī, who possesses the luster of the moon, somehow assumed the form of a woman and departed from Kṛṣṇa while he was asleep on his bed of water; or, having become afraid, she dwells in the house of a king, having taken the form of another woman? (3)
How can I, having begun, continue to reflect? What shall I do now? For my mind does not function according to my will. Indeed, in this matter:
Though forbidden with effort, it does not look away for even a moment;
it follows its long-practiced path, just as a scripture that has been poorly mastered [is forgotten]. (4)

Or rather, it is not possible to conquer the mind. I shall simply think about her. Oh, what a convergence of all feminine virtues in one place! (He sits down, overcome with thought. (Then enter the nurse and Nalinikā. Nurse: (Reflecting) Oh, what a difficult situation for the task at hand! If it is done in this way, the royal palace will be disgraced; if it is not done, she will certainly perish. By me...
It has been investigated through many means, yet even now she conceals it from me. And what of her concealment? From that time forward, she no longer desires garlands or cosmetics;

she has no longing for food; she finds no pleasure in the company of friends; she sighs deeply; she speaks incoherently; she does not understand what is said to her; she laughs secretly; she weeps in solitude; she feigns illness; she becomes emaciated and turns pale. There is one thing more wonderful: despite such particular conditions, out of shame and fear for herself—
Out of family pride and her youthful nature, she does not speak even to one person. (Alas, the difficulty of this matter! If it is done in this way, the royal household will be disgraced;

if it is not done, she will surely perish. I have deliberated upon many means, yet even now she conceals [her feelings] from me. Or rather, what need is there for her to conceal them? From that time forward, she has had no desire for flowers or cosmetics, she has no longing for food, she finds no pleasure in the company of social circles, she sighs deeply, speaks incoherently, and does not respond to what is said to her.)

She knows [her state], she laughs in secret, she weeps in solitude, she feigns illness, she becomes thin, and she turns pale. There is one thing even more wonderful: because of her modesty, her fear, her sense of family honor, and her youth, she does not speak of anything to even a single person regarding such particular conditions of her own. Nalinikā: Why does she not speak? She tells me everything.
Dhātrī: Friend! I know your intention; having understood her condition, [the King] said, "In every way, unite her with this man.
Nalinikā: Could one such as this, possessing such distinguished qualities, possibly be of low birth?

Dhātrī: But there is doubt in that matter. I heard near the Queen that the ministers indeed said, "He is not of such a low birth; he conceals his identity for some reason. Nalinikā: Who, then, could it be?
Dhātrī: If that doubt does not exist, who else could be a son-in-law of such superior qualities?
(Behind the scenes:
Even if there were wealth, beauty, knowledge, courage, and the like, yet for those deficient in lineage, there exists no purity of conduct.
"You will certainly hear of his lineage here when the time comes; abandon your suspicion regarding his family, for this matter must be accomplished, as it has a happy conclusion. (4)
Nurse: Friend! Who indeed said that?
Nalinikā: No one at all is seen here. Nurse:
My body’s hair stands on end. Without a doubt, it was spoken by fate. Moreover, I know that this is no mere mortal.

Nalinikā: His family background is uncertain. I wonder whether he will follow our advice or not. (Reflecting) That person is truly fortunate that he can drive her to such madness! To say more, even the God of Love himself would suffer upon beholding the princess's beauty; therefore, I suspect that he too must be suffering. (He has gone; his family background is uncertain. I wonder whether he will follow our words or not. That man is indeed blessed who thus drives her to distraction. What more need be said? Even the Lord Kāmadeva himself would suffer upon seeing the princess’s form; therefore, I surmise that he too suffers.)
What more need be said? Even Kāmadeva himself suffers upon beholding the beauty of the princess; therefore, I suspect that he too suffers because of her.
Nurse: Friend! This is his residence, the one we came to out of curiosity on the day of the elephant-panic.
Nalinikā: Friend! Oh, how beautiful and well-adorned is the entrance! Friend! Come, let us enter. (Friend! How beautiful and well-adorned is the entrance! Friend! Come, let us enter.)

Dhātrī: Friend! Where is the young master? What do you say? "He is in the quadrangle. (Walking about and looking) Here is our young master, all alone, standing and pondering something. Nalinikā: Friend! Let us enter then.
Nurse: Let us do so. (Entering) Welcome to the noble sir! (Let us do so. Welcome to the noble sir.
Avimāraka: Oh, what a perfection of beauty she possesses! Nurse: (Agitated) What indeed could it be? Welcome to the noble sir! (What indeed could it be? Welcome to the noble sir!)
Avimāraka: Her chest is languid from the weight of her breasts, and her body is exhausted by the burden of her hips.
Dhātrī: Oh, she is delirious! (Ammo, vippalavadi.
Avimāraka: [Her face] is the delight of the eyes, with lips naturally as red as the bimba fruit.

Dhātrī: Blessed indeed is that person who can thus intoxicate him. Avimāraka: If even in fear his body remains such a vessel for the drinking of my eyes— Dhātrī: Then the task is well accomplished. Avimāraka: Even in fear, if his body remains such a vessel for the drinking of my eyes— Dhātrī: Then the task is well accomplished.
Avimāraka: How indeed could that [union] possess such abundant grace characteristic of the intervals between bouts of love-making?
Nurse: She herself is the one who drives him mad; she alone is the one who maddens him.
Nalinikā: Well said—that he too will suffer.
Nurse: You have understood it well. May the noble sir be happy.
Avimāraka—(Looking at them with bashfulness) Welcome to you both. Both—Is all well? Avimāraka—It will be so by the sight of you both.
Nurse: Noble sir! What is being contemplated? Avimāraka: Madam! A treatise is being contemplated.
Nurse: What indeed is this delightful science that is being contemplated in this secluded place?
Avimāraka: My lady, the treatise on Yoga is being considered.
Nurse (smiling): Your auspicious words have been accepted. Let it be the Yoga-śāstra indeed.
Avimāraka (to himself): What, indeed, is the meaning of her words? Under the influence of my own desire, I imagine it to be something else. (Aloud) What is your intention, lady?

Nurse: Desiring a union, we have come. Since a union has been approved by the Noble One, our task is indeed finished, for there is a secluded space in the royal palace. Even there, someone remains contemplating the union even more intensely; therefore, let the Noble One contemplate the proper arrangement of the union right there with him. (Desiring a union, we two have arrived. "A union has been approved by the Noble One"—surely our business is concluded, for there is a secluded opportunity in the royal palace. Even there, a certain person remains contemplating the union even more intensely.)
"Reflecting on this, let the noble one consider how to properly apply the methods of yoga right there with him.
Avimāraka: How is it that even now my fortunes remain? (Rising from his seat) Noble lady!
My life has been restored to me as if given back once more. Why is this so?

Beholding her face—whose glance was a poison agitated by fear, yet charming and gentle in appearance, yet exceedingly sharp—I had long been driven to madness; but today, by the nectar of your words, I have once again been restored to consciousness. (7)

Nurse: By good fortune, this person has been protected by the noble sir. Enough of further delay; the inner apartments must be entered this very day. The minister Āryabhūtika, the guardian of the inner apartments, has been honored by our Great King along with the messenger of the King of Kāśī and has set out.

Avimāraka: Very well; that is the first course of action. Madam, what patient ever recovers after obtaining the medicine? Nurse: Entering alone is already difficult; it is possible to stay inside for a long time. Avimāraka: Once I have entered, I should be considered as having arrived. Let the palace row be made free from obstacles and spacious.

Nurse: Let us do so. We shall complete all the internal preparations. May the noble sir enter with full attention. Avimāraka: Madam! Please tell me once more the arrangement of the royal palace. Nurse: It is just as follows.
Avimāraka: Alas, sir!
Having heard of the king’s arrangements for his residence, my mind realizes that I have entered [his domain].
Human effort indeed should not be disparaged,
provided that fate does not lead to its failure.
(Reflecting) Lady! What proof do we have for this matter?
Both—This is the proof. Victory to the noble son! (This is the proof. Victory to the noble son!
Avimāraka—Ah, let us depart now. Let it be awaited until midnight.
Both: Whatever the noble lord commands. (They exit.
(Then the Vidūṣaka enters.

Vidūṣaka: Oh, how beautiful the city looks today! The divine sun has reached the zenith; he is seen upon the palace rooftops, white as lumps of curd, and amidst the forecourts of the market stalls where sweet-smelling garlands are displayed.

The courtesans and the citizens, adorned with their respective finery and desiring to display themselves, move about with graceful coquetry in various palaces. But I, having gone out from the city because I wished to be a companion for my noble lord while he was being driven mad by seeing such sights, have found that—alas for our misfortune—he has become as if transformed by some evil thought. This is the noble lord’s residence. Today, in the courtyard of the city market, I heard that the noble lady...

The king’s daughter has come out from her house with her nurse and her friend. What indeed should be done here? Or rather, men’s fortunes are as fickle as an elephant’s trunk. Or rather, let this misfortune befall us; I shall enter the royal palace, which is suited to my condition. (Entering) Oh, oh! Here comes the noble sir, as if anointed with the very essence of the desires of lovers by his pale complexion. Or rather, every ornament becomes beautiful people. (Approaching) Victory to you, sir! (Ah, how magnificent is the city’s splendor at this moment!)

The Blessed Sun, having reached its setting, is seen like molasses spread out upon the palace rooftops and shop-fronts, which are as white as balls of curd. Both the courtesans and the citizens, desiring to display themselves adorned with their respective finery, move about restlessly in those various palaces. But I, becoming intoxicated by such sights, thought, "I shall be the companion for His Honor during the night," and thus departed from the city. Yet, through our misfortune, he too has become as if changed by some ill-considered calamity. This is it.

This is the residence of His Honor. Today, in the arcade of the city marketplace, I heard that the nurse and the friend of the princess have departed from His Honor’s house. What indeed could be the matter here? Or rather, the fortunes of men are as fickle as the trunk of an elephant. Or let this misfortune befall us; I shall enter the royal palace in accordance with my station. Ha! Ha! Here comes His Honor himself, appearing pale as if smeared with the cosmetic of a lover. Or perhaps, for those who are handsome, everything serves as an ornament.
"May you be victorious!
Avimāraka: "Friend! You have been far too long in the city.

Vidūṣaka: "As for you, you are like a Brahmin who, having forgotten his invitation, broods over it day and night. As for me, I have been wandering through the city all day long, yet I have not found a courtesan who will grant me food."

"Having passed the night in pleasure, I am returning. (You, meanwhile, like a Brahmin deceived by an invitation, brood over it day and night. I too, having wandered through the city during the day without obtaining any enjoyment, come back at night to sleep by your side like an ordinary courtesan.
Avimāraka: "Friend! I shall tell you something pleasing."
Vidūṣaka: Is our curse from the sage finished?
Avimāraka: You fool! When a matter is destined to happen, what cause for joy is there?
Vidūṣaka: What else could it be?
Avimāraka: Were the nurse Kuraṅgī and Nalinikā not seen?
Vidūṣaka: Yes, sir! Those ladies were seen. What was brought?
Avimāraka: The medicine for my sorrow has been brought.
Vidūṣaka: I shall see for myself.
Avimāraka: You will see in due time; for now, listen.
Vidūṣaka: Let my lord speak, let him speak!
Avimāraka: What more need be said? Her Highness says that the maiden’s quarters must be entered this very day.
Vidūṣaka: (Laughing) By what means indeed do you intend to enter the interior and seize her alive? The ministers of Kuntibhoja are, by their very nature, of treacherous character.
Avimāraka: How can you also have such doubts? Behold:
by me alone, the enemies along with their armies were shattered; even now they do not approach out of fear of my scent.
What need have I for mere humans? Even that lord of the asuras, though possessing a deformed appearance, was slain by me with my own two arms.

Vidūṣaka: I know, I know; your deeds are superhuman. However, entering another's house under the cover of night is in every way to be suspected. Avimāraka: This is the summary. In any case, I must enter the maiden’s quarters of Kuntibhoja. Therefore, may the great Brāhmaṇa grant me his permission.
Vidūṣaka: How can you go away, abandoning me? I never leave your side. Even if he reviles me, a single companion is to be desired. Avimāraka: You do not understand the path of the scriptures.
One should go alone to another's house, but deliberate with a second;
one should engage in battle with many—such is the conclusion of the treatises.

Therefore, I alone must enter Kuntibhoja’s inner apartments for women. You should not have any suspicion toward us; behold, O Lord, how the army of Kuntibhoja is well-guarded, yet this royal palace can be entered easily with its riches and comforts.
Moreover, O friend, we are primarily armed with our own arms; why then should we be suspected by you? (11)

Vidūṣaka: If this is the decision you have made, then let us enter the city now. I have a friend there; we shall wait for some time at his residence. Avimāraka: You speak rightly. Having entered the interior now, performed our daily rites, and received permission from the Great King, we shall enter the sleeping quarters where the bed is prepared, and then, remaining unrecognized, enter the city.
"I shall wait for the time at your friend's house. (Entering) Maid: Victory to the young master! The bath-water has been brought. (Victory to the young master! The bath-water has returned.)
Avimāraka: Here I come; go on ahead.
Maid: As the young master commands.
(Exit) Avimāraka: Friend! The blessed sun has set. For now—
The eastern quarter is smeared with darkness,
while the western direction shines red with twilight;
the intermediate space of the sky is divided into two parts.
...which possesses the splendor of the form of Ardhanārīśvara. || 12 ||
Vidūṣaka: You speak truly, sir. Day has passed; night has arrived.
Avimāraka: Oh, how wondrous is the nature of the world! For why?
The sun, the tilaka-mark upon the face of the sky, has been wiped away; the garland of stars has spread abroad.
With its heat vanished, its breezes soft and enchanting,
and with lovers withdrawn while heroes roam abroad, the world of men seems to be assuming a different guise.
(Both exit) End of the Second Act.
The Third Act begins.
(Then enter Kuraṅgī and two maidservants. Kuraṅgī: Friend! What was said by him?
Maid: Princess! By whom?

Kuraṅgī—(To herself) Alas, I am indeed unfortunate! (Aloud) By the servant of the inner apartments! (Alas, I am indeed unfortunate! By the servant of the inner apartments! Māgadhikās—The servant of the inner apartments was seen by me, and he was spoken to; yet he said nothing.

Kuraṅgī—Ah, I shall inform the Queen: "The servant of the inner apartments will not attend to my parrot-cage. (Ah, I shall inform the Queen: "The servant of the inner apartments will not attend to my parrot-cage.")
[She] says: "Is it finished? Māgadhikā: "Indeed, the parrot-cage for the princess is finished.
Kuraṅgī: "Talkative woman! Is there another as well?"
Māgadhikā: It must be so. Kuraṅgī: Friend! What time is it?
Māgadhikā: The evening has deepened.
Kuraṅgī: In that case, let us ascend to the palace.
Māgadhikā: O playful lady! Go ahead; prepare the beds and seats. Vilāsinī: You are already asleep! What time is it for preparing the beds and seats?
Māgadhikā: Friend! I know your laziness. You say that things were prepared during the day when they were actually prepared at night. Vilāsinī: Friend!
Do not speak thus. Apart from the Princess, things are quite different.
[They are there.
Friend! I shall go and find out. (Friend! I will go and see.
(All walk about.)
Māgadhikā: This is the palace.
Kuraṅgī: Go ahead. (She mimes ascending. Go forward.

Māgadhikā: Well done, playful lady! Well done! You have acted in a manner worthy of your own name. Here is a bed prepared upon this stone slab. (Well done, playful lady! Well done! It is made to match your own name.)
It is done. A bed has been prepared upon this stone slab.
The playful women say: "The bed has indeed been arranged in the inner pavilion, O Māgadhikā! Look, look at my languor! (abhyantaramaṇḍape khalu racitaṃ śayanaṃ, Māgadhike!
paśya paśya me 'lasatvam).

Māgadhikā: She has indeed become very clever! May you obtain a husband whose conduct is like that of a wise servant. (She has indeed become very clever! May you obtain a husband whose conduct is like that of a wise servant.
Kuraṅgī: Friend! I shall sit for a moment on this stone slab.
Māgadhikā: Whatever pleases the princess. So be it.
(All sit down. Māgadhikā: Noble lady, I shall deliver the exposition.
Kuraṅgī: Friend, I know your incoherent prattle.
Māgadhikā: Noble lady, this is indeed a fresh story!
Kuraṅgī: I beg you, do not press me; let me sleep for a moment. Vilāsinī: May the noble lady sleep in peace. Tell it to me.
Kuraṅgī—(To herself) What indeed could it be?
Māgadhikā—Friend! Listen without the princess hearing.
Kuraṅgī—Ah! The secret is known. I am undone!
Vilāsinī: Friend! Where did you hear this?
Māgadhikā: It was told by Vasumitrā, the attendant of the Queen.
Vilāsinī: So it was the Queen herself who told it?
Māgadhikā: There is a son of the King of Kāśī named Jayavarmā; the princess has been given to him. His messenger arrived and was honored by the Great King, and the dowry was accepted.
Kuraṅgī—(To herself) This is false; I am my own mistress.

Māgadhikā—It is said that the Queen spoke thus: "My daughter is indeed young; I cannot live even for a single day while watching her [in distress]. If the Great King is pleased with me, the son-in-law must be brought right here. (There, it is said the Queen spoke—"My daughter is indeed young...")

[She] cannot live without seeing [him] by day. "If the Great King is pleased with me, my son-in-law must be brought right here. Vilāsinī: And then? And then? Māgadhikā: Then that too was indeed approved by the Great King. Saying, "Today is an auspicious constellation," the minister Ayyabhūdia was dispatched by him as a messenger. And then... that too... was indeed approved by the Great King. [Thinking] "Today is an auspicious constellation," the minister Ayyabhūdia was sent by him as a messenger.

"It was indeed approved by the Great King, for he said, 'Today the constellation is auspicious,' and by that messenger, the minister Āryabhūtika has been dispatched. Kuraṅgī: (With joy) Ah, this matter has been delayed! Vilāsinī: It is pleasing that the beauty and youth of the Princess have now become fruitful.

(Entering) Nalinikā: My mother told me, "Go and tell this news to the princess. Even pleasant things become even more dear when they are announced by those who love us. But she, too, seeing me, will not say everything with full confidence. I, however, shall have the power to speak at the right time. I must go and announce this pleasant news to the princess. (She walks about.)

(For my mother said: "Go and tell this news to the princess; pleasant things, when announced by one who is dear, become even more pleasant. Moreover, she herself, while seeing me, does not feel entirely confident. I too shall have access to her side at the right time so that I may announce what is pleasing to the princess.

Kuraṅgī: What indeed is this unprecedented sorrow that, when brooded over, drives me to distraction? She does not desire the *sumanā* garland; she finds no pleasure in the assembly. This is both cruel and charming in this matter.
(Sighing) Nalinikā! What is this?
What unprecedented malady, when brooded over, drives me to madness? She desires no garlands or cosmetics; she finds no pleasure in conversation. This is both cruel and heart-wrenching.
Nalinikā! What is this?

Nalinikā: I am Nalinikā. Indeed, the mistress has been informed by the sound of the steps. Mistress! The lady says this.
Kuraṅgī: What? Nalinikā: (In her ear) It is as follows.
Kuraṅgī: Alas, my conduct has been base!
Nalinikā: Surely this is to be expected; surely it is he himself!
Kuraṅgī: Nalinikā! Massage me!
Nalinikā: As the princess commands.
Vilāsinī: Nalinikā! When will the wedding take place?
(Offstage)
Today Nalinikā— may you live long!
(Behind the scenes)

"O royal officers! A certain servant of the minister has not arrived to guard the inner apartments, as the minister has departed. Therefore, let it be as you wish; meanwhile, I shall inform the King tomorrow.
Vilāsinī: Friend Nalinikā! What was said?
Nalinikā: When that noble son enters, then the marriage will take place.
Vilāsinī: Enter without hindrance. (Enter without hindrance.
Nalinikā: So be it.
Māgadhikā: Friend! Come, let us sit in the quadrangular hall. (Friend! Come, let us sit in the quadrangular hall.)
Vilāsinī: So be it. The evening has almost passed; the moonlight has risen. Nalinikā: Friend! Spread out a bed for me as well.
Māgadhikā: There is space. Attend upon the princess until she falls asleep.
Nalinikā: So be it. (Thus it shall be.
(Both exit.
Then enters Avimāraka, sword in hand and wearing the guise of a thief, with a rope in his hand.)
Avimāraka—(Reflectively) Oh! Alas, what a thing is youth! For why?
It causes passion to swell, it resorts to negligence, it disregards faults, and it embarks upon rashness.
It wanders according to its own will and does not desire the path of righteous conduct; it overpowers the auspicious intellect of even the most learned. || 1 ||
Why should I falter in matters that depend solely upon myself?
For here, I am well-acquainted with the city; the guards are known to me; the night is deep and terrible with its dense darkness; my sword is a reliable companion and my inner soul is resolute.
What need is there for much deliberation? What task could possibly be difficult for me to accomplish? (2)
Oh, the terrifying nature of the midnight hour! For now, all creatures have fallen into a stupor like those still in the womb;
the palaces are as silent as people sleeping peacefully, as if they have entered into deep meditation.
As if seized by accumulated darkness, the mountains can only be inferred by touch; the entire world, its form concealed, seems to vanish from sight. || 3 ||
Truly, the night of doom has begun this very day;
the rows of mansions appear like sandbanks upon the rivers of the road, bearing a darkness as if it were flowing water.
In the darkness, the ten directions have their forms submerged;
this gloom is as if it were a river to be crossed by swimming. || 4 ||

(Walking about and placing his hand to his ear) Ah! A sound like that of a lute is heard. Who indeed is this man, ever-happy, who enjoys the music of a lute together with his beloved? Clearly, he is playing the lute himself. Why so?
For the resonance of the strings is heard echoing loudly from the latticed windows of the lofty palace.
What power do the fingers of a woman's hand have to clearly employ such an external posture? (5)
The dull sound, having become clearly manifested, arises through the mouth and nose;
even though it is coarse, the cause is the sound of clapping hands.
It is produced by the sound of the bracelets. || 6 ||

(Walking about and looking around) Ha ha ha! Who else is this who seeks to appease his angry beloved? It must be some great offense against Ravalva, since she does not become placated even at this hour. Or rather, this Ravalvi is already appeased and merely desires a pretext. Why so?
With her throat choked, dulled, faltering, and crooked by tears,
she spoke incompletely out of affection, "What am I to you?"— she who, though brought under the power of her beloved through his true devotion, remained thus.
From the state of being female, she speaks only what is disagreeable. || 7 ||

"Who indeed is this bird with such a terrifying cry? Ah, it is surely an owl! How is it that he laughed? This poor creature must have been embraced by his beloved, who was terrified upon hearing the sound of the owl. It is fitting for one of his age. Why concern himself with observing the affairs of others? Let us depart for now. (Walking about) Who indeed is this person here in the courtyard of the city marketplace, speaking so apprehensively yet so affectionately?
This poor fellow is surely a fellow student of mine.
He is oppressed by his attendants; he speaks softly as if agitated by the tinkling of his ornaments;
overcome by passion, he speaks of union as something that brings no pleasure.
He desires the conventional agreement, yet he does not desire to enter into it. || 8 ||

(Walking about) Ah, this is moonlight! This is not moonlight; it is the glow of lamps passing through the lattice windows of the palaces situated in both rows. Here indeed, one must protect oneself with great effort. Ah, but here is a thief!
For he—his heart gladdened by the firm binding of his waist-knot—
With his gaze and movements fixed upon the dwelling of another,
though moving swiftly, he watches for the light of a lamp and remains fearless of treading upon it.

Ah, I shall evade him. (Standing aside) That cruel man has gone away. We too shall now depart. (Walking about) Ah, these are indeed guards! What indeed shall I do now? Very well, I have seen a way. I will enter this assembly of libertines at the crossroads. (Leaping over and standing there) But the guards, whose prowess is limited, have turned their faces away.
"Having approached me, this sword of mine seems to laugh;
these guards are merely a burden to me, for I have entered here intent on accomplishing my purpose. (10)
The guards have departed; who protects one whose self is unprotected?
Having joined a faction of few men, they roam at night with valor, yet possessed of passion, greed, and delusion.
But here, the nocturnal wanderer is a witness to the essence of human effort, and his course through the night is both very uneven and pleasant.

This is the royal palace! Oh, the stability and height of this wall! Indeed, here men must gird their loins. Or rather, I should consider myself as having already entered, if these parapets are firm. Standing here, I shall cast down the rope. Homage to Prajāpati! Homage to all the Siddhas! May Bali, Śambara, and Mahākāla be gracious!

May the night expand; may sleep increase; may Padmā grant her permission; may all obstacles come to rest; may adversaries be destroyed. May the Blessed Kātyāyanī be victorious! (Throwing the rope) Ah, the turret has been secured by the crab-shaped rope! Oh, the power of destiny! With a single throw, I see the rope perfectly fastened, like the very accomplishment of my purpose. Oh, how powerful indeed is the Blessed Lord of Creatures! For why?
If success is not achieved despite effort being made, what fault is there in this?
Or rather, one performs action thinking, "Who is it that does not succeed for me?
Through auspicious efforts, manliness arises here among men.
The accomplishment of an undertaking follows the decree of fate. || 12 ||
"Very well, I shall climb by taking hold of the rope. (Having climbed and looked) Oh, the splendor of the royal family!
This palace of the king, though vast, appears as if measured; through its divisions it seems dense, yet it rises in gradual height, adorned with a row of hundreds [of pillars].
It seems as if the earth wishes to go to the sky. || 13 ||

But one must not remain here; from the watchtowers, the gateways, and the royal highways, all manner of obstacles arise. Very well, I shall descend by this very rope. (Having descended) Where indeed shall I hide the rope now? (Reflecting) Very well, I have seen it. I shall cut the tether in this elephant stable and throw it away. (Throws it; walks around) Ah!
This is the sound of lute strings accompanied by the soft singing of young women.
I shall go elsewhere.
Ah, this is the fragrance of ichor, sharp with the rutting-fluid of a noble elephant!
Having stayed for a moment, I shall depart.
The light of these lamps is spread here, yet what can these guardian men do?
After a long time, the royal palace has become tranquil at night along with its clusters of lotuses.

I shall go. This is the path she described; here is the Mandākinī; that is Mount Dāruparvataka; this is the assembly hall. Ah, here is the palace of the maidens' quarters. Since it abounds in wooden structures and has latticed windows nearby, it is easy to climb. Or, even if it were difficult to ascend, what cause for hesitation could there be for me, whose mind—driven by longing for my beloved—is already intent on a righteous ascent?
Who here, with a mind terrified by the thorns on the entwined stalks and tormented by thirst, would abandon a lotus pond? (14)

"Very well, I shall ascend. (Having ascended) "This is the mechanical lattice-work mentioned by her. (Opening it, entering, and looking about) "Excellent, Kuntibhoja! Excellent! By this building, heaven itself seems to be mocked; for indeed:
Swans sleep upon slabs of precious gem-stones, while the expanse of its sands is composed of beryl and pearls."
The pillars are fashioned from coral; what is the use of these idle words? Lamps struck down by the light of jewels grow dim. || 16 ||
Enough with this fierce attire! (Removing the thief’s disguise, he unties his waistband.

Nalinikā: What indeed is the news concerning the young master? And the young mistress, too, finds sleep difficult to obtain due to her condition; yet today, she has found it merely upon hearing that "my beloved is coming."
Avimāraka—(Hearing this, approaching suddenly) Lady! This is my story.
Nalinikā—(Looking at him, with joy) Welcome to the noble youth! (To herself: To the noble youth.
Avimāraka—(Seeing her, with delight) Here she is, here she is, she for whom I—
The gaze is not satiated, as if embracing her very limbs; the mind hastens, as if awakening her from sleep;
passion impels her, as if causing her limbs to sink.
Through joy, the inner self becomes serene and yet also bewildered. || 17 ||
Nalinikā—(To herself) This venerable Lord of Love truly afflicts both sides like a torrential flood. (Aloud) My lord! Let the couch be adorned.
Avimāraka—Very well. (He sits down.)
Nalinikā: My lord, shall I awaken my lady?
Avimāraka: Good woman, enough, enough of this childish fickleness! Behold, I have but two eyes, not a thousand.
And my intellect, long yearning for it, has today seen the further shore of the ocean of desire;
let my pair of eyes rejoice in happiness. 18.
Nalinikā: I know, I know that the young master’s fatigue was on account of the young mistress. Avimāraka: Today my labor has borne fruit.
Kuraṅgī: (Having understood) Friend! Why was such a thing said so heartlessly?
Nalinikā: My lady, I indeed said so previously.
