"What did I say?
Nalinikā: "Noble lady, nothing was said.
Avimāraka: "This second delusion of mine arises from the expansion of her own delusion."
Kuraṅgī: Nalinikā! We have indeed been sitting here for a long time. What hour is it? Nalinikā: It has become midnight.
Kuraṅgī: In that case, you must be exhausted. Come, embrace me.

Nalinikā—(Aside) I shall massage her. My lord’s son! Embrace my lady! (Ahaṃ saṃvāhayāmi| Bhartṛdāraka! Pariṣvajasva bhartṛdārikām|) Avimāraka—(With joy) Very well. In this very way, may you too hear hundreds of pleasant things. Kuraṅgī—Enough of this excessive affection. Come now. (Alam atisnehena| Ehi tāvat|)
Nalinikā: Noble lady, here I am.
Kuraṅgī: (Forcibly pulling Avimāraka toward her and embracing him) Ah! Who is it that massages me now?
Nalinikā: (Into her ear) It seems to be so.
Kuraṅgī—(With agitation) Alas! My character is ruined! I am terrified!
Avimāraka—Not so, my beloved! You are not new to me. Why do you tremble from the assault of my mind, like a creeper struck by the force of the wind?
O blessed lady! Abandon your fear and show me favor; what is the use of much lamenting? I have come to you for refuge. (19)
Nalinikā: My lord, rise, rise! The princess says, "Rise, indeed.
Avimāraka: Very well. (He rises.)
Nurse: Victory to the young master!
Avimāraka: What, is it you?
Nurse: Nalinikā! The bed has been prepared in the inner pavilion; lead both the young lady and the young master there. (Nalinikā! Indeed, in the inner pavilion...)

The bed has been prepared. Have the princess and the prince enter right there. Nalinikā: Very well. (The nurse exits. Nalinikā: My lord! The bed has indeed been prepared in the inner pavilion. Let the prince enter there together with the princess.
The bedchamber. Let him enter there together with the princess.
Avimāraka: You too shall hear hundreds of such pleasant things. (Taking her hand with his own, he rises.
Nalinikā: This way, this way, my lord! (Etvetu bhartṛdārakaḥ.)
Avimāraka: Here I come, my dear friend. (Both walk about.
Avimāraka: (With joy) I am now free from the debt of my youth. For why?
My eyes are overflowing with tears, and my hands are grasping my heaving breasts.
Her hips are heavy with burden, her feet lack clarity, and they falter with shame;
this, O friend, is the measure of our seven steps!
If this union were to last for a hundred ages instead of a single night, who else but me would be so blessed? (20)
(All exit. End of the Third Act.
The Fourth Act begins.
(Then enters Māgadhikā, carrying a basket in her hand.

Māgadhikā: Oh, the negligence of the attendants! Not even until sunrise has the arrangement of the palace been made. The clamor of the people gathered for conversation is not heard. What could this be? Ah, perhaps they are fast asleep at dawn because of staying awake all night. I shall wake the young mistress of the house. (She walks about. (Oh, the negligence of the attendants! Not even until sunrise has the arrangement of the palace been made. The clamor of the people gathered for conversation is not heard. What could this be?)
Ah, having stayed awake all night, she must have fallen asleep at dawn. I shall wake the young mistress.
(Then enters Vilāsinī with a fan.
Vilāsinī: Māgadhikā! Stop, stop! (Māgadhikā! Stay, stay!)
Māgadhikā: Friend, do not stop me! I am bringing flowers and cosmetics for the princess. Vilāsinī:
What need has the princess for flowers and cosmetics, or for ornaments?
Māgadhikā: You ill-mannered girl! Do not speak such inauspicious things. Let the princess always be adorned!
Very well.
Vilāsinī: I do not mean that the very appearance of the princess is her ornament; I say that her appearance itself is her ornament. Māgadhikā: O madwoman! Surely even a flower is scented?

Vilāsinī: This is fitting; things that are naturally beautiful become exceedingly lovely when adorned. Māgadhikā: Friend! Truly well-matched is the husband chosen for the princess, one who is worthy of her beauty.
Vilāsinī: Enough with this partiality; near the young master, the young mistress appears like a lotus.
Māgadhikā: She speaks well. I too think that the Blessed One Kāmadeva must be such a person when he possesses a physical body.
"Kāmadeva must be like this. Vilāsinī: "In that very way, the princess does not find delight even for a single moment without the prince.
(Then enters Nalinikā, weeping.)

Nalinikā—(With sorrow) Truly, the worldly proverb is true: "Happiness is beset with many obstacles. This year has indeed passed for the princess in joy, having been filled with uninterrupted enjoyment of pleasure. But for us, her companions, it has become like a residence in Uttarakuru. Today, upon hearing that this news has been reported by the Great King, my body seems to sink. And the princess, overwhelmed by bashfulness and confusion, has become as if senseless from distress. As for this palace...
It appears to me like a lamp that has been extinguished. Since I have been separated from my noble son, not even a single thing has occurred that brings joy to my heart.

Hearing today that the noble son has departed without obstacle, my heart is as if filled with delight. At present, Kanyakubja is well-guarded. (Walking about) Oh, my friends! Dear Madhukarikā, what is this?
(The popular saying is indeed true: "Happiness is beset by many obstacles. Indeed, this year has passed for the princess without her enjoying uninterrupted happiness. Rati—
Having done so, our circle of friends has come to dwell in Uttarakuru. Now, having heard that this news has indeed been learned by the Great King today, my body seems to sink with grief.

And the princess, struck by shame, fear, and passion, has become bewildered by her fever, as if she were deprived of her senses. Indeed, this palace appears to me like one whose lamp has been extinguished.

It occurs to me that since I have been separated from my lord’s son, not even a single thing has brought joy to my heart. Hearing that my lord’s son has departed without obstacle, my heart is as if gladdened today. Now, the maidens’ quarters are strictly guarded. Oh, friends!
Halā Māgadhikā! What is this? Māgadhikā: Friend! Why do you ask? Is it not the time for the lady’s adornment?
Nalinikā: The festival has passed! (She weeps. (The festival has passed.
Both: Is this like a dream? Speak, so that we may be comforted! (Is this like a dream? Speak, so that we may be comforted!
Nalinikā: The young master has departed for good! (The young master has departed for good!)
Both: We!
Nalinikā: I too have come here, unable to bear witnessing the suffering of the noble lady.
Māgadhikā: Indeed, it is not possible to witness the condition of the noble lady. Nevertheless, we shall comfort her.
"Nevertheless, we shall comfort the princess.
Both: "We will do so.
(They all exit.)
(Then enters Avimāraka.
Avimāraka—(with sorrow):
How have I managed to escape from the maidens' quarters and come here?
Relying on nothing but my body and the remnants of my fortune,
even now my mind does not come to me, nor does it regard me, being occupied by that beloved of mine. || 1 ||
What indeed would be the condition of the doe?

She would be ashamed by the rumors of the servants, terrified by being firmly confined by the king, and with eyes clouded by tears and not looking toward me, she might fall into a swoon during the nights; what shall I do? (2)

Ah! A remedy has been found. Nevertheless, for my sake, he did not spare his own life; therefore, I too shall now sacrifice my life for his sake. (Walking about) I have been away for several days, but today both my mind and body seem to me as if they cannot endure this suffering. For here, [I see] her whose passion increases through a sincere acquaintance—

Having abandoned her—who was rich in beauty, in the bloom of fresh youth, and charming—for even a moment, I have been cheated while still alive; what other kind of wretched ingratitude could there be in this world? (3)
For now, as I am being consumed within by Love, the divine thousand-rayed sun has begun to turn bitter. (Looking all around) Oh, the terrifying nature of the summer heat!
For now, the earth is exceedingly hot, as if feverish from the rays of the sun, its essence having been sucked dry.
Like trees afflicted by consumption, their shade stolen away due to the proximity of forest fires,
the mountains— with the mouths of their caves wide open as if crying out in helplessness—
seem to cause this world to fall into a swoon, its heart destroyed by the ripening heat of the sun.
What shall I do now? Nor am I able to go. Why?
Harsh winds smear [the world] with particles of sand and fire; the mountains cause perspiration with their rough foliage.
The sun, its body melted by forest fires, seems to flow; the world, shaken by the heat of the sun, seems to bear fruit [of exhaustion]. (5)

"Alas, my beloved! Alas, O beautiful one! Give me an answer! (He acts out fainting. Then, sighing again and looking upward: "The divine sun, with its thousand rays, is indeed obstructed. Or rather, what is so strange in this? The clouds have spread abroad."
Do they not indeed obstruct the sun when driven by the wind?
If they were to ward off my desire situated within me, that would be truly marvelous. || 6 ||

What is the use of this living death? I shall abandon my life. (Rising and walking about) What indeed shall I do? Very well, I have found a way. I shall abandon my life in this forest pond. Shame! My path to death is truly unrighteous; through the delusion of pride, the great highway has been forgotten. I shall strive by another means. (Looking around) Very well, I have found it. Ah! A forest fire is seen not far away. Into that I shall offer my life as an oblation. (Approaching and bowing) O Blessed One, Agni!
If fire shall accomplish the desired goal for those of one mind,
then in the next world as well, that beloved of mine shall be known by a single name.
(Entering with curiosity) What is this that is happening?
The trees fall, consumed by masses of sparks,
yet my flames are as cool as the paste of Malaya sandalwood.
For Agni shows compassion even toward one afflicted by passion, and embraces him with joy like a father his son. || 8 ||

Oh! What can be more wonderful than this? Truly, fire does not burn me. Or rather, there is a reason for this as well. Otherwise, I shall try [to escape]. (Walking about) This indeed is a great mountain, its peaks indistinctly visible as they mingle with masses of dark clouds.
Serving as a place of rest for the flocks of birds that roam the sky,
variegated by the intellect of a skilled poet and heart-pleasing through its association with a friend,
it appears like a base king— rich yet fruitless.

"Let it be; I shall give up my life on this mountain, for a leap from the cliff accomplishes all goals. I will now climb. (Having climbed and looked around) "Here is the water situated at the cow-pasture; having bathed and sipped it, I shall mutter the mantra. (Having done so, he mutters).
(Then enters a Vidyādhara with his beloved).

Vidyādhara: In the past, the morning twilight was spent in the northern Kuru lands; having bathed again in Lake Mānasa, youth was made to blossom once more upon the slopes within the caves of Mount Mandara.
For the sake of sport, we wandered through the caverns of the Himavat, and our gaze was captivated.
We two shall go to the sandalwood trees of the Malaya mountains, which offer the pleasure of midday sleep.

(Examining the aerial chariot) Saudāminī! Look, look at the beautiful form of the divine Earth standing afar! For here, the great mountains are like young elephants, the oceans like pleasure ponds, the trees resemble water-moss, and the surface of the earth has its depressions and elevations concealed.
The mountains appear like hair-partings, the vast palaces like drops of water,
and the entire world, seen in its contracted form, shines as if it were a mere curve.
"My dear lady, be attentive; we shall go to Malaya, the abode of cool sandalwood.
Saudāminī: "Noble sir, so be it. (Both gaze toward the sky-chariot.)
Saudāminī: Noble sir! I am unable to go on without resting. Vidyādhara: In that case, we shall rest for a moment on some mountain and then depart.
Saudāminī: Noble sir! This is pleasing to me.
Vidyādhara: Saudāminī! Look, look!
The earth, marked by the ocean, seems to rush toward it with speed as if abandoning the dense mass of clouds;
and these [clouds] are like the waters of the rainy season.
The mountains, expanding forth, shine intensely.
"Madam! This mountain seems capable of providing us with hospitality for a moment. Therefore, we shall go there to rest.
Saudāminī: "Noble sir! Let us do so. Vidyādhara: "Saudāminī! It is our duty to take a sixth part of the blossoms from the flowering trees. Therefore, we shall leave the trees free from debt."
Saudāminī: Noble sir! So be it.
(They both act out gathering flowers.

Vidyādhara: (Looking at Avimāraka) Ah! Who indeed can this be? Ah, I have recognized him. This is surely a Vidyādhara who has fallen from his spells. For what reason? Such a form does not belong to others. Fortunately...

Since he has been seen, let me ask about what I have forgotten. Avimāraka: Very well; the task for the gods is accomplished. I shall descend. (Looking to the side, seeing a Vidyādhara) Ho! Who indeed is this? Or rather, this must be a dream; for I am not asleep. Ah, at the time of death, men see all sorts of things; this might be such a thing. But even that belongs to those who are utterly deluded; as for me, I know everything. Very well.

I shall ask him: "O sir! Of which lineage are you the ornament? The Vidyādhara: Listen—"I am a Vidyādhara named Meghanāda, and this is my wife, Saudāminī by name. Today, a festival has been commenced on Mount Malaya by the Vidyādharas to worship the venerable Agastya. We too were invited there; having descended here with the thought that we would rest for a moment before departing, such is our story. Now..."
"For what purpose do you now turn this surface of the earth into the world of the gods?
Avimāraka—(To himself) What indeed should be said? Since my end is at hand, I must not speak a falsehood. (Aloud) O sir! I am Avimāraka by name, the son of the King of Sauvīra.

Vidyādhara: (To himself) This is a falsehood. This form is not human. (Aloud) Now, for what purpose have you come here alone? Avimāraka: (To himself) What indeed shall I say? (He stands with his face cast down. Vidyādhara: (To himself) Very well, I myself shall find out. (He invokes a spell. O! Alas! This son of the blessed Agni does not know himself.

Desiring and taking pleasure with Kuraṅgī, the daughter of Kuntibhoja, he departed once his presence there was discovered; finding no means of re-entry and longing to give up his life, he has climbed here to commit suicide by leaping from the cliff. She too experiences a death-in-life there. I shall be your companion in this matter. (Aloud) O Avimāraka! True friendship indeed means being without guile. You are not able to conceal a matter that is known to me.
Avimāraka: Let it be said.

Vidyādhara: From this day forward, let there be friendship between us. Furthermore, we have learned of all your circumstances; indeed, you have ascended here for the purpose of abandoning your life. Avimāraka: Friend, it is even so.
Vidyādhara: Oh! I am pleased by this confidence. If there were a way to enter there unobserved, what would you do?
Avimāraka: (With joy) What else? I shall enter. For that is the very purpose of my distraction.
Vidyādhara: Then, my friend! Look at this ring. (He shows him the ring.)
Avimāraka: Friend, what is the use of this?
Vidyādhara: Wearing this ring on the right finger, one becomes invisible; with the left, one remains in one's natural state.
Avimāraka: Friend, I have that too.
Vidyādhara: I shall provide you with proof of this. Friend! Do you see me?
Avimāraka: Indeed. Vidyādhara: Pay close attention.
Avimāraka: I am attentive.
Vidyādhara: (Pointing with his right finger) Friend! Do you see me?
Avimāraka: Friend! Not even a shadow is visible; how much less the body? Indeed, these are the ones who are called happy in this world.
Those who travel through the sky accompanied by women,
who sport on mountain slopes having received instruction,
and who, though knowing everything through the powers produced by mantras, wander at ease— both invisible and visible.
"Very well; I have indeed entered by an improper means. The Vidyādhara—(placing it on his left finger): "In that case, let this ring be taken.
Avimāraka—(taking it): "I am favored."
Vidyādhara: No, no; I alone am the one favored. Why?
A virtuous person does not rejoice so much upon obtaining a jewel as he does when, having given it away, he bestows it upon a worthy recipient whose desires are directed toward that very object. (14)
Avimāraka: But I have one doubt. To say that it should be tested on my body seems, as it were, improper.
Vidyādhara: In that case, place it upon your right finger.
Avimāraka: Very well. (He does so.)
Vidyādhara: Friend! Take up your sword.

Vidyādhara: As you wish, friend! It is certain that when one is invisible (*antarhita*), and when one touches what is invisible, and when one touches that [which was touched], then one becomes invisible.
Avimāraka: Friend! I am pleased. This is prosperity upon prosperity. Friend! I suspect it has been delayed because of our regard for one another. Let there be no further delay now.
Vidyādhara: I have entered, provided that you permit me. Avimāraka: What is the use of speaking at length?
For those like you who possess mastery over the sciences (vidyā), [nothing remains hidden].
Who like me would desire to repay such a favor?
I am purchased by the gift of my life; command me, your servant—what shall I do? (17)
Vidyādhara: I know your guileless intellect. If you will follow my word, inform my friend of me, and remember me, O friend! Behold my departure.
Entice the princess with these games; I shall be by her side again during other tasks. 18.
"Aho! This very essence of manhood indeed does not wish to let go of my heart. Friend, let us depart for now.
Avimāraka: "May you go, for the sake of seeing each other again.
Vidyādhara: "Certainly. (The Vidyādhara rises together with his beloved.)

Avimāraka— (Looking upward) Here indeed is the venerable Meghanāda, plunging into the ocean of the sky. He is he whose hair at the crown is tossed by the wind, whose body-unguents are smeared by the hollows of the clouds,
whose waistband is firmly tied, and whose slender waist is touched by the hands of his beloved young woman.

With his upper garment fluttering in the wind, crushing the stars with the clusters of gems on his crown, this glorious Vidyadhara proceeds, diminishing as he moves with the speed of flight through the upper realms. || 19 ||
This woman also follows her beloved by the power of her magic science— she whose side-locks have become loose and disheveled from the speed,
and whose slender waist is sinking, exhausted by the heaving of her breasts.
In the sky, with her upper body previously offered by her beloved,
she was seen and then vanished like lightning among the clouds.
The honorable Meghanāda has departed. I too shall set out toward the city this very day. Until I descend... (having descended) I am as if exhausted. Very well;
having rested for a moment upon this stone slab, I shall go. (He sits down.
(Then the Vidūṣaka enters.)

Vidūṣaka: Oh, what misfortune for the King of Sauvīra, whose name is so well-chosen! Having long been childless, he obtained through his own special vows and the grace of the gods a noble son, rare even in the world of men; yet, having regained him, he has become just as he was before. In every way, it is my own failure to complete my life’s purpose and the misfortune of my kinsmen that the prince has been lost. (Walking about) Today, indeed, the lady said, "The prince has gone safely. But who here knows? He is exceedingly delicate.
"Rāvaṇa, being tormented by the god of love, has become skilled in wandering about. I too shall search the entire world until I find either the prince or the prince’s body;
if I do not see him, I shall become an ally to His Honor in the afterlife. I am indeed exhausted. Very well, I will rest for a moment in the shade of this tree and then depart.
(He falls asleep. "Oh, how fortunate is His Honor, the King of Sauvīra, whose name is auspiciously invoked, who—having been childless for a long time—[attained his own son]..."

Having obtained, through specific religious observances and by the grace of fate, a virtuous son who is rare in the world of men, he has once again become just as he was before. Yet, due to the exhaustion of my own life-span and the misfortune of my kinsmen, the prince has been lost. Indeed, today the lady said, "The prince has gone in safety. Or rather, who here knows whether the exceedingly delicate prince, struck down by the god of love while alone, remains safe after being lost? As for me, I shall seek either the prince or the prince's body.

"I shall first wander about and observe the whole world; if I do not find [him], then I will become an assistant to His Honor in the next life. I am indeed exhausted. Very well, having rested for a moment in this shade of a tree, I shall depart. Avimāraka: What state indeed is this for one who is satisfied? It would be excellent if my departure had been heard by him; if it has not been heard, that Brahmin will perish. Or rather, what is it to me?
Without him, all undertakings are in vain;
for he is a laughingstock in social gatherings, a mere soldier in battles, a source of grief to his elders, and a reckless man toward his enemies.
A great festival is in my heart; what is the use of further lamentations? Indeed, my body has been divided in two.

(Looking all around) Ah! Who indeed is this traveler sleeping in the shade? (Approaching) What a joy for my heart that he has come by chance! My mind hastens to embrace him. Vidūṣaka: (Waking up) I have indeed slept for a long time! I shall go now. What rest can there be for those whose desires have been shattered? (Walking about and looking at Avimāraka) How is it that it is His Highness?
Avimāraka: (I have indeed slept for a long time. I shall now depart. What rest can there be for those whose desires have been shattered? How is it that you, the honorable Avimāraka, are here?

Avimāraka: Ah, my friend, you are well-contented! (Both embrace each other. Vidūṣaka: (Laughing loudly) O friend! Tell me, tell me! What have you done during all this time? (O friend! Speak, speak! What have you done during all this time?)
[It is done.
Avimāraka: Friend! This has been done. (Having slipped the ring onto his right finger, he withdraws it.
Vidūṣaka: Alas, alas! Where, where is His Honor? Why is he not seen? Because of my constant anxiety for him, I seem to see him even now. Or rather, I shall make it clear. O friend!

"You are cursed by a curse, if you hide yourself! (Hā hā! Where, where is His Honor? Why is he not seen? Alas! Because my thoughts have gone toward him, I see him as if he were right here. Or rather, I shall make it clear. O friend! You are cursed by a curse, if you hide yourself.
Avimāraka: Friend! Here I am.
Vidūṣaka: Where, where are you?

Avimāraka: (Throwing his ring onto his left finger) Friend! Here I am. Vidūṣaka: Previously you were Avimāraka ("Unconquered"), but now you have become Māyāvimāraka ("Concealer by Deceit"). O master of illusion! Why do you not wander through the city of Kanyākubja in disguise? Vidūṣaka: First [you were] Avimāraka, now you have become Māyāvimāraka. O master of illusion! Why do you not roam about in the city of Kanyākubja in a concealed form? [First...]
The pure Avimāraka has now become a deceiver of Māyā. Thus, O deceiver of wealth! Why do you not move about in the maidens’ quarters in disguise?
Avimāraka: Friend! Now indeed this has been discovered.
Vidūṣaka: Wonderful, wonderful! Whence has this come to him now?
Avimāraka: I shall tell everyone in the inner apartments.
Vidūṣaka: Now you are hungry. (Now you are hungry. Avimāraka: You fool! Come quickly for entry into the place of execution. This hand must not be released at all.

Vidūṣaka: Wonderful, wonderful! Even I am invisible; my body exists or does not exist—I shall leave it as a remnant. *Thu thu!* Avimāraka: You fool! Enough, enough with this delay! My mind is in haste to see my beloved. (He draws her toward him.)
Vidūṣaka: I have no faith in it.
Avimāraka: Well then, I shall wait for the time of the meal. Vidūṣaka: After resting for a short while, we shall go.
Avimāraka: Does Kuraṅgī not remember me?
Vidūṣaka: How indeed can the scentless female ascetic still be alive?
Avimāraka: Friend! I entreat you; please come quickly.
Vidūṣaka: Why are you hurrying like a bridegroom who has completed his student life? (Why are you hurrying like a bridegroom who has performed the rite of returning home after his studies?
Avimāraka: You fool! Just wait here for a moment. Vidūṣaka: Do not pull me; here I am following you. (Do not drag me; here I am running after you.)
Avimāraka – (Walking about) Here is the city. Vidūṣaka – I shall first behold the splendor of the city. Avimāraka – This is the royal palace.
That you, filled with apprehension at night, committed such a rash act by entering this royal palace,
and then again today during the day, having secured good assistance— [this is indeed astonishing].
I enter without hesitation, like a skillful man entering a crowd of the virtuous. || 22 ||
(Walking about) Now, Kuraṅgī must have bathed and be staying inside the palace.
Vidūṣaka: Let us enter anywhere or other; the time for alms has passed. Avimāraka: Come, let us enter right inside. (Entering) For here—
It is easy for those wise men who previously dwelt happily in their own homes, having come here with thoughts of what was difficult to attain,
and who have now achieved their purpose with joyful hearts, to enter again comfortably, especially since they have performed meritorious deeds. || 23 ||
(They both exit.
The Fourth Act.
The Fifth Act.
(Then enter Kuraṅgī and Nalinikā. Nalinikā: Noble lady, enough with this distress! Let us ascend the palace of the maidens' quarters and divert our eyes [with sights].

Kuraṅgī: Friend! Have you truly understood my heart? For here, these most fragrant flowers—such as the *bakula*, *sarala*, *sajjajjuṇa*, *kadamba*, and *nīpa*, all beloved by the rainy season—which are being brought by my attendants who do not understand, drive me to madness for the sake of pleasing me. Moreover, these peacocks cause excessive agitation in our royal palace-minds; even the female parrot, though cooing with us, displays her own nature as a serpent-lady because she does not know the proper place and time. Even the maina has begun to deliver nothing but a lecture.

"Even Bhūtikārikā, unaware of my state of despondency, has come thinking she would tell me all the news of the world. My attendants have also arrived to inquire after my health, but they report to me only by way of flattery. Therefore, I wish to remain in the palace for a moment. (Friend! Have you truly understood my heart? For here, these most fragrant flowers—beloved of the rainy season—such as *bakula*, *sarala*, *sarja*, *arjuna*, *kadamba*, *nīpa*, and *nicula*, being brought in by my attendants who do not understand my condition, only serve to drive me to madness in their desire to please me.)"
Moreover, these peacocks are acting as if they were the very lords of our royal household. Though constantly cherished by us, they display an air of superior knowledge, ignorant of time and place.

Even the parrots and mainas have begun to deliver formal expositions. Without considering my state of despondency, even Bhūtika the maina has arrived, thinking, "I shall recount the news of all the world.
My attendants, having come to inquire about my illness, importune me and press their reports upon me. Therefore, I wish to sit in the palace for a moment.
Nalinikā: Whatever pleases the young lady, let it be so.
(Both ascend. Kuraṅgī: Friend! Even here a great calamity has arisen—a dark cloud bearing a lamp of lightning. (Halā! atrāpi mahān anartha utthitaḥ vidyutpradīpaṃ dhṛtvā kālameghaḥ.)
Kālamegha:
Nalinikā—Noble lady, enough with this longing. Look, look at the expanse of the sky, where the sun is obscured by fresh rain-clouds and which is beautiful with the falling of sparse drops of water.
Kuraṅgī: And I see that the sky is beautiful. (Then enter Avimāraka and Vidūṣaka.
Avimāraka: Friend! I have seen that Kuraṅgī; she is this one—
Free from illness and from unseasonable aloe and sandalwood ointments, with her ornaments cast off and her coquettish gestures gone,
she shines with limbs that are charming in their natural simplicity.
The Vedic revelation is like a reason devoid of its logical ground.

Vidūṣaka: Oh! I am pleased! You indeed flatter yourself, thinking, "I am handsome in the eyes of all the world. But you have now been surpassed by her, whose beauty is charming by its very nature. I imagine she has become so thin due to separation from you; yet even so, she delights me like the crescent of the new moon.
"Even so, she delights the sight like the crescent of the new moon.
Avimāraka: "Friend! You speak like one who is far too wise. What is this?
Vidūṣaka: "O! You mock me with your constant familiarity. A person never seen before praises my intellect all the more because he does not understand it. I too shall make that known in this city."
"I do not place my trust in anyone. "Sir! You mock me because of our constant acquaintance. A person who is unfamiliar with me praises me excessively, not knowing my character.
Having realized this, I no longer place my trust in anyone in this city.

Avimāraka: Enough of this indifference. Because I am surrounded by many people, I have not found the opportunity to awaken my beloved. Therefore, now we shall go to the palace and awaken her right there.

Vidūṣaka: You speak well, sir. Let us ascend the palace. (suṣṭhu bhavān bhaṇati | prāsādamārohāvaḥ |) Avimāraka: Friend! One must ascend with such care that the sound of the palace does not arise. Vidūṣaka: Oh! This is impossible. Who can eat without leaving some crumbs? I shall stay here; you alone ascend. (bhoḥ! na śakyametat)
Who would dare to eat without first clearing away the leftovers? I shall remain here; you yourself must climb up.
Avimāraka: If I let go, you will be seen.
Vidūṣaka: Oh! I have indeed forgotten this. Tell me again and again. (Bhoḥ! Vismṛtaṃ khalu mayaitat | Punaḥ punaḥ kathaya |)
Avimāraka: This way, please. (Having climbed up and looked around) Friend! There sits our beloved upon the stone slab together with Nalinikā.
She is there, resting her dejected face upon her left hand, unable to endure the passage of time, that companion of the Mind-born God.
Distraught, she ponders something with a steady gaze, looking upward to restrain her tears.
Kuraṅgī—(To herself) What is the use of this living death?
(Aloud) Nalinikā! Go and bring Māgadhikā with the bath-water.
Nalinikā—How can I go, leaving the young mistress all alone? Surely there is no one here.

Indeed, someone is here. (Entering) Hariṇikā: Victory to the young mistress! Young mistress, the lady says: "What kind of headache do you have now? You must apply this medicinal ointment. (Victory...)
The Princess: "Princess! The lady says: 'How is your headache now? She also says to apply this medicine.
Kuraṅgī:
"Nalinikā! Go now. I suspect it has begun to rain. I wish to bathe in the fresh water from the sky; therefore, hurry with my bath-water."
[With haste, she prepares for the bath. Nalinikā: "Whatever the young mistress commands. [Yad bhartṛdārikājñāpayati.
Avimāraka: "What indeed has she resolved to do?"
Kuraṅgī: Friend! Come here for a moment. Nalinikā: Noble lady! Here I am.
Kuraṅgī: Friend! Indeed, your body is cool.
Nalinikā: Noble lady, I do not know.
Kuraṅgī: Friend, come, embrace me!
Nalinikā: Noble lady, so be it. (She embraces her.)
Kuraṅgī: Friend! Your body is exceedingly cool and enchanting. Nalinikā:
I am favored.
Kuraṅgī: Friend! Now my bodily fever seems to vanish. (To herself) Ah, I have performed my service; today my contact with her body is at an end.
(Aloud) Go now, then. (Friend! My bodily fever seems to be subsiding at this very moment. Alas, my friend’s affection has been shown; today, too, my contact with her body has come to an end.
Go now, then.
Nalinikā: As the princess commands. (Exit) [Yad bhartṛdārikājñāpayati.]
Hariṇikā: Noble lady, what shall I report to the Queen?
Kuraṅgī: That today she is free from illness and restored to health.
Hariṇikā: When asked how you knew this, what am I to report?
Kuraṅgī: You have understood it well. Say, "By means of this specific medicine.
Hariṇikā: As the young lady commands. (Exit.
Avimāraka: What indeed has she resolved to do?
The slender-limbed woman breathes hotly and looks about repeatedly;
with her eyes filled with tears, what indeed is she resolved to do? (3)
Kuraṅgī: Very well; I shall hang myself with my upper garment and put an end to my life. (Rising and doing so, she hears the thundering of clouds: Ah! Save me, save me!
Avimāraka: Friend! It is not possible to remain indifferent beyond this point. (Placing the ring on his left finger: My beloved! Do not fear, do not fear! (He raises Kuraṅgī up.)
Kuraṅgī—(With joy) Could this really be true? I have become as if deluded.
Avimāraka—Beloved, let your apprehension be dispelled. (He embraces her.
Kuraṅgī—How wonderful! In a single moment, the burning of my body seems to vanish.
Avimāraka: This embrace of hers, though familiar through constant practice, possesses a greater intensity than our first union due to the application of my mind;
it is like the victory experienced today by a king through daring at the head of battle.

Vidūṣaka: How is it that she has begun to weep? Enough of this excessive distress! Or rather, I too shall weep. Even a single tear is difficult to extract from my eyes. When my father passed away, I began to weep with great effort, yet not even a tear would come forth; how much less so now under this other affliction? Nevertheless, I weep without being moved by passion. How is it that she has begun to weep? Enough of this excessive distress! Or rather, I too shall weep. Even a single tear is difficult to extract from my eyes. When my father passed away, I began to weep with great effort, yet not even a tear would come forth; how much less so now under this other affliction? Nevertheless, I weep without being moved by passion. (Kathaṃ roditumārabdhā | Alamatimātraṃ santāpena | Athavā ahamapi rodimi | Ekamapi tatra durlabhaṃ mama nayanād bappaṃ na nirgacchati | Yadā me pitā uparataḥ, tadāpi mahatā ārambheṇa roditumārabdhaḥ | Bappaṃ na nirgacchati kiṃ punaranyasantāpasya | Tathāpyanuśśuo rodāmi |)
Tears do not flow. Even when my father passed away, I began to weep with great effort, yet tears would not come; how much less so now for this other sorrow?
Nevertheless, I weep without longing.
Avimāraka: Enough of this mockery! For that which is called affection is indeed free from deceit.
It is not that my intelligence is to be censured by you, whereby I am made an object of your ridicule at will; for in the application of action, both the wise and the foolish are alike.
The body attains equanimity, but the intellect does not. || 5 ||

(Entering) Nalinikā: Hariṇikā! Hariṇikā! Why is the door blocked? Alas! I fear that by blocking the door she will cause herself further torment. Hariṇikā! Hariṇikā! Oh, alas! That very thing has indeed happened. (Hariṇikā! Hariṇikā! How is it the door is blocked? Alas! I suspect that by blocking the door she will bring about her own cessation of suffering.)

"Hariṇikā! Hariṇikā! Alas, woe! That very thing has come to pass! Avimāraka: This is the voice of Nalinikā. Friend, let the door be opened! Vidūṣaka: As Your Honor commands. (Opening it) Come, come, Madam! (yad bhavānājñāpayati | etvetu bhavati |)
Nalinikā: Who is this man now? Vidūṣaka: You have understood perfectly! Oh, the distinction of the royal court! What other person, upon seeing me, would say, "This is a man"? I am indeed a woman.
Avimāraka: Nalinikā! Enter now. Nalinikā: How is it that the young master is here? Young master! I salute you. Young master! Who is this man?
Vidūṣaka: I am the maidservant named Puṣkariṇī.

Avimāraka: This is that Brāhmaṇa who is always said by us to be "satisfied. Vidūṣaka: Yes, lady! By his sacrificial thread he is a Brāhmaṇa, and by his saffron robe he is a Raktapaṭa. If I remove my garment, I become a Śramaṇa. Lady! What is this? (Amā bhavati!)

"A Brahmin by his sacred thread, a red-robed monk by his saffron robe. If I remove my garment, I become a mere ascetic. My lord! What is this? Nalinikā: "It is the ceremonial bath for the noble lady. Vidūṣaka: "What need is there for this ceremonial bath for a lady who is weeping from hunger? Go quickly and bring food; I shall be the first to eat."

"What is the use of this bath-water for my noble lady, who is hungry and weeping? Go quickly and bring food; I am to be seated at the head of the table. Nalinikā: "O wicked Brahmin! You are even thinking of food? Let all that wait for now. How could the young master have entered the royal highway during the day, when it is crowded with many people?"

Avimāraka: Being satisfied, he will tell you everything. Nalinikā: I am dismissed by these words of great respect. Very well; taking this [gift], I shall enter the four-winged hall and hear the news from the company of friends. Come, Brahmin! (She draws him toward her. (I am dismissed by these words of great respect. Very well; taking this, I shall enter the four-winged hall and hear the news from the company of friends. Come!)
Brāhmaṇa!
Vidūṣaka: An outrage! An outrage! (A most un-Brahmanly thing!
Kuraṅgī: This Brāhmaṇa is indeed laughable! (He is truly ridiculous!)
Avimāraka: Friend, you are indeed laughable!

Vidūṣaka: Who here says anything untrustworthy of me? I am not the laughingstock; rather, it is the lady herself who is laughable, she who, having recognized her own condition and resolved to do something, forgot everything upon hearing the sound of thunder and fell down. (Who here says anything untrustworthy of me? I am not the laughingstock; rather, it is the lady herself who is laughable...)
Having resolved to do so, she heard the sound of the clouds and fell down, forgetting everything.
Kuraṅgī: Ah, even this was seen by these two!
Nalinikā: I beg you! Come here, O Brahmin!
Vidūṣaka: If you give me food, then I shall go; it is customary to give food to a guest.
Nalinikā: Come, I will give you all my ornaments.
Vidūṣaka: No, bile is not cured by words of consolation. Place it into my hands.
Nalinikā: So be it. (Having removed her ornaments, she gives them to him. Vidūṣaka: Listen, lady. (Listen, madam.)

Nalinikā: You fool, you Brahmin! Having sat down in the four-pillared hall, I am listening along with the members of the assembly. I shall return after asking her ladyship. Nalinikā: Who are you, who have become my beloved by taking all my ornaments? Wait a moment! (She seizes the Vidūṣaka by the hand. Who are you, who, having taken all my ornaments, have become my beloved?
[He has] been born. Come now.
Vidūṣaka: Madam! Do not say so! I am indeed very delicate.
Nalinikā: I know, I know your delicacy. If you are so delicate, come quickly!
Vidūṣaka: Lady! Here I come. (They both exit. Avimāraka: My dear, look, look at these most beautiful clouds of the rainy season, so dear to the time of the monsoon! For these—

The clouds are the drummers for the proclamation of the rainy season, performing various forms of magical illusions; they are the plows of Indra, the curtains for the stage of the starry sky, and have become the anthills for the serpents that are the lightning-flashes.
They are the whetstone-shafts for the arrows of Love, the gatekeepers for the enraged women, and the water-pots for bathing the mountains.
The dark clouds shine like celestial water-stations and mechanical fountains, drawing their alms of water from the ocean and opening the gates of the three worlds.
Kuraṅgī: Noble Lord! They have now become beautiful to behold.
Avimāraka: Oh, how vast and yet how sparse are the showers! For indeed, the streams fall like the waves of the ocean of the sky.
Like the frowns of a woman to be guarded, flashes of lightning quiver;
the time has arrived for the crushing of the firm breasts of the prime of youth.
Kuraṅgī: Noble Lord! The god has now begun to rain.
Avimāraka: My dear, come, let us enter within. Kuraṅgī: (With joy) As the noble lord commands.
(They both exit.
The Fifth Act.
The Sixth Act.
(Then enters the Nurse.

Nurse: Oh, what a lack of stability on the part of one who has reached the end! For the King’s daughter was first betrothed by the Great King, the King of Sauvīra, to Vihana-sena. Yet today, she has formed a connection with someone born this very day, possessing extraordinary qualities rare in the world of men. And now, there is the son of the King of Kāśī named Jayavarman.

The noble lady Sudarśanā, together with the minister Bhūtika, has been sent off and has now entered the royal palace. It is said that the King of Kāśī himself did not come because of his sacrificial duties. What indeed could this mean? (Alas, how unstable is the course of destiny! For first the princess was chosen by the Great King, the sovereign of Sauvīra, for the sake of Viṣṇusena;

yet today she has been united with some person of unknown birth, whose form and distinguished qualities are difficult to find in the world of men. And now there is this son of the King of Kāśī named Jayavarman.)

"He was brought by the queen Sudarśanā and the minister Bhūtika, and has now entered the royal palace. It is said that the King of Kāśi himself did not come because of his preoccupation with the sacrificial rites. What indeed could this mean? (Then enters Vasumitrā.)

Vasumitrā: Oh, how inconsistent are the astrologers! They think only of their own particular lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and do not understand the gravity of the task. The prince entered today, and the wedding was appointed for this very day. (Walking about) Why is it that Jayadā, appearing as if displeased, seems to be brooding over something? Jayadā! The Queen says—"Come here. (Aho viṣamaśīlāḥ sāṃvatsarikā nāmātmano nakṣatraviśeṣameva cintayanti, karmagauravaṃ na...)

[They] know: "The prince entered today; the wedding was appointed for this very day. Why indeed does she appear dejected and anxious, as if thinking of something that must be told to Jayadeva? Jayadeva!
The lady says: 'Come'.
Nurse: "Friend! Do you know what the reason is? [Friend: "Do you know what the reason is?"]
Vasumitrā: What else? One must consider what ought to be done regarding this matter.
Nurse: What is the Queen’s intention at present?

Vasumitrā: Without knowing the condition of Vihanasena, who is born of her own lineage, she does not wish to give her daughter to Jayavarman; however, the Great King, unaware of the son of the King of Sauvīra...
"Today, it is said, great distress has arisen. (Not knowing the condition of Viṣṇusena, who is born of his own lineage, [the King] does not wish to give his daughter to Jayavarman.
However, the Great King, not knowing that he is the son of the Sauvīra king, has today indeed become greatly distressed.
(Entering)

Nalinikā: Today all our difficulties seem as if they have been met with a rendezvous. (Walking about and looking around) Why indeed does my mother here appear to be deliberating on something with Vasumitrā? I shall approach her and hear the unpleasant news.

Vasumitrā: Friend Nalinikā! Come here for a moment. You know the affairs of the royal court because of your living together with the chamberlain. Nalinikā: It is a recent development; indeed, I have come to inform you of it.

Vasumitrā: Speak, my child! Nalinikā: Indeed, an envoy has been sent by the ministers of the King of Sauvīra [with this message]: "Our lord is living incognito in your city, together with his sons, wife, and attendants. Thus, let our master be informed of this news by our secret agents.

"Let our secret agents find out the news, Master, as to whether he is living in disguise. Both: "How so? That he is living in disguise? Then what then? Nalinikā: "Then, having heard all this and having seen the conclusion of that letter, it is said that the Great King went with the noble Bhūrivasu to search for him. (Then all this...)
Having heard the conclusion of that letter, it is said that the Great King, together with the noble Bhūtika, has gone to search for him. Nurse: What indeed could this be?
Vāsulmitrā: Nalinikā! You, meanwhile, enter the inner apartments.
Nalinikā: As the noble lady says. (Exit: "As the noble lady says. Vasumitrā: Come now, let us go see the mistress.
Nurse: Let us do so.
(Exeunt. (Then enters Kuntibhoja with Bhūti and the King of Sauvīra.
Kuntibhoja: Friend!
Why do you gaze at my face? You have not been seen for a long time; embrace me firmly, friend! Remember our childhood, when I would look upon you with affection and unblinking eyes.
Today, our friendship has been renewed by affection, as if made new once again. || 1 ||
The King of Sauvīra: Whatever you desire.
(Both embrace.
Kuntibhoja: My mind seems to be overwhelmed by anxiety, and my speech is faltering, choked with tears.
Your eyes are filled with tears and your face is not serene; why do you manifest such distress at a time for rejoicing? || 2 ||

The King of Sauvīra said: "Indeed, I am not unglad at the sight of you; rather, it is this powerful thing called affection for one's son. That grief which has been dwelling within my heart since my departure from the city expands today, and having found you as its companion, it has issued forth in the form of tears. (3)
Kuntibhoja: Why this grief concerning my son? Bhūtikas: Let it be known by my lord; indeed, the prince has not been seen during this past year.
Sauvīrarāja: There is such a thing as powerful affection for a son. Please consider this.
Today I think of my son Avimāraka, who possesses incomparable strength, vigor, and beauty,
his hair-tips sprinkled with the dust of your feet.
If he were here, who indeed would be superior to me? || 4 ||
Bhūtika—(To himself) This great distress indeed increases all the more without the Prince. I shall dispel it. (Aloud) How is it that calamity has befallen my master?
Kuntibhoja—I too, due to this distraction, forgot to ask about this.
The King of Sauvīra: Listen; or rather, Bhūtika knows. Does he wish to hear it from my mouth? Kuntibhoja: We are attentive.
The King of Sauvīra: Is it known that there is a Brahmin-sage named Caṇḍabhārgava, who is exceedingly wrathful?

Kuntibhoja: It is heard that the venerable Kuntibhoja, a treasure-house of asceticism, is the king of Sauvīra; he has arrived in our territory. However, in the forest, his disciple was killed by a tiger.
Kuntibhoja: What happened after that? What happened next?

Sauvīrarāja: Then, at that very time, I too arrived at that place by chance while out on a hunt. Kuntibhoja: And then? What happened next? Sauvīrarāja: Then, upon seeing me, his face became distorted with a frown of rising wrath; he had a mass of long matted locks hanging down, and placing his hand upon his disciple, he was as if burning with the fire of anger, desiring not to hear my words.
With his speech faltering due to agitation, he began to reproach me in many ways.

Kuntibhoja said: "And then? And then? The King of Sauvīra replied: "Then, because of the overwhelming power of destiny, I became impatient and grew enraged, saying, 'You do not tell the story; you revile me without cause!'"
You do not speak; you fall into anger without cause; you cast [us] off excessively. You are a vessel for austerities, yet through your provocation—
Through you, who appear in the form of a Brahman seer, this dog-cooker [shall become one].
Kuntibhoja: You have spoken what is unbecoming.
Sauvīrarāja: Then, upon hearing that, like the divine Fire-god sprinkled with a stream of clarified butter, his eyes blazed and, shaking his head repeatedly while exclaiming, "How?
How?", he began to curse me because I, a preeminent Brahman-sage, was addressed as a dog-cooker (śvapāka).
Therefore, you, along with your sons and wife, shall attain the state of a dog-cooker.
Thus [spoke] Kuntibhoja: "Oh, how great is the danger that arises from even a small root! Bhūtika said: "Fortunate is the royal house of Sauvīra! Why so?"
At that time, because the Brahman-sage was enraged, he was turned into a dog-cooker (outcaste);
therefore, he was not reduced to ashes in that very form.
Kuntibhoja: You have spoken rightly. What happened after that?

Sauvīrarāja: Thereafter, my mind agitated by his curse, I entreated him for a long time until, gradually returning to his natural state, he granted me this favor: "As long as you remain in disguise, you shall dwell in a cow-pen for one year."
Then, when a full year has passed, you shall be released from the curse.

Thus he spoke. Having said this, with a serene mind, he called out, "Come, O Kāśyapa! That young boy, following him, was killed by a tiger. And for one year, I observed the vow of a dog-cooker (outcaste). Today I am released from the curse.
Kuntibhoja said: "Oh, how calamities arise and how they cease! By good fortune, you have prospered."
Bhūtika: Victory to my lord!
Kuntibhoja: But surely Viṣṇusena’s mother has entered the inner apartments along with her attendants? Bhūtika: Her Majesty, having entered within, awakens a long-dormant affection.
Kuntibhoja: Now then, how did Viṣṇusena become Avimāraka?
Bhūtika: Let my lord listen—there was an asura named Dhūmaketu. While wandering about for the purpose of slaying all the worlds, he once set out to destroy the kingdom of Sauvīra.
Kuntibhoja: This is indeed an unprecedented tale! What happened next? What happened after that?

Bhūtika: Then, seeing the suffering of all the subjects in that place of affliction and disregarding any remedy for that *rākṣasa*, the Lord fell into distress. Kuntibhoja: What happened after that? Bhūtika: Then, having learned of all that, Prince Viṣṇusena—his limbs roughened by the dust of the earth, his side-locks hanging down—while playing with boys of his own age, by the turn of fate...
While the guards were negligent, he suddenly arrived at that place where the Rākṣasa was.
Kuntibhoja: Oh, what a marvel! And then? Bhūtika: Then that Rākṣasa, beholding the prince—who appeared like a perfectly prepared meal—out of delight began to perform his task.

Kuntibhoja: Oh, what cruelty on the part of the Rākṣasa! And then? What happened next? Bhūtika: Then the prince, having laughed slightly, [struck him] like the falling thunderbolt strikes the king of mountains.
Just as a forest region is consumed by a forest fire,
so was that base man slain in battle by that prince, who, though unarmed, acted with ease.
Kuntibhoja: At the very first, during the panic caused by the elephant, I said that this boy was produced by fate and is not merely human.
Sauvīrarāja: How can you, who possess the wisdom of a thousand eyes, think thus regarding Avimāraka through your spies?
Bhūtika: My Lord!
I have thoroughly examined all accessible regions, yet the prince is not seen anywhere by my spies; nevertheless,
I possess the mental capacity to investigate him.
For it surely follows after illusion. || 10 ||
Nārada said: With the Vedas I satisfy the Grandfather (Brahmā); with songs I cause the hairs on Hari’s body to stand on end;
day after day, by means of various methods, I produce discordant clashes among the musical notes on stringed instruments within the world.
"O! We have been honored for a long time by Duryodhana, the father of Kuntibhoja! Now that he has returned to his human nature, Kuntibhoja treats us as mere servants.

Today, a great crisis has arisen for Kuntibhoja and the King of Sauvīra due to the failure to see Avimāraka. Therefore, I have now descended to earth to resolve their distress by revealing Avimāraka. (Thus, he stands before Kuntibhoja and the King of Sauvīra.)
Kuntibhoja: Ah, it is the blessed celestial sage Nārada! Blessed one, I offer my salutations.
Nārada: May it be well with you.
Kuntibhoja: I am graced by your presence.
Sauvīrarāja: Venerable sir, I salute you.
Nārada: May there be peace for you.
Sauvīrarāja: Venerable sir, I salute you.
Nārada: May peace be with you.
The King of Sauvīra: I am favored.
Kuntibhoja: (Into the ear) Bhūtika! Let it be done thus.
Bhūtika: As my lord commands. (Exit and re-enter) Here is the water for washing the hands and the water for the feet.
Kuntibhoja: Blessed one, please do me this favor.
Nārada: So be it.
Kuntibhoja: (Having honored him) Blessed One! Our home has been purified by your descent here.
Sauvīrarāja: Now I am released from the curse, having beheld the divine sage.
Nārada: It was not for the sake of seeing you that I came here at this time; rather, having learned of the suffering caused by the harassment of Avimāraka, I descended [to this world].
Both: If that is so, we are freed from our distress.
Nārada: Bhūtika, bring Sudarśanā here.
Bhūtika: As the Blessed One commands. (Exit and re-enters with Sudarśanā.)
Sudarśanā: The divine seer has arrived.
Bhūtika: Indeed.
Sudarśanā: Now my son’s marriage has become well-provided for. (Approaching) Blessed one, I salute you! Now my son’s marriage has become well-provided for. Blessed one, I salute you!
[He bows.
Nārada: "It is even so, O illustrious lady! May you always enjoy joy, and may King Kuntibhoja always be filled with affection for you. (12)
Sudarśanā: I am favored.
Nārada: Now, may you two ask whatever is to be asked. Both: We are favored.
Kuntibhoja: Blessed One, does the son of the Sauvīra king still live?
Nārada: Indeed he does.
Sauvīra King: For what reason is he not seen?
Nārada: Because of the interruption of the wedding. The King of Sauvīra: How has the prince been entertained?
Kuntibhoja: In what region, then?
Nārada: In the city of Vairantya.
Kuntibhoja: There is indeed a city named Vairantya. Very well; with whom has he entered into the relationship of son-in-law?
Nārada: With Kuntibhoja.
Kuntibhoja: Who is he?
Nārada: He is the father of Kuraṅgī, the king who rules over the city of Vairantya;
surely you are Kuntibhoja, the son of Duryodhana. 13.
Kuntibhoja: What is the use of many questions? It is said by your reverence that he has taken pleasure with my daughter Kuraṅgī.
Nārada: It is even so.
Kuntibhoja: I am as if ashamed. By whom was she given to him, or how? And how did he enter the inner apartments of the maidens?
Nārada said: She was previously given away according to the prescribed rites; she was seen during the confusion caused by the elephant.
Having first relied upon his manly prowess, he entered [the city] again by means of his illusory power.
Kuntibhoja: Let it be so; for the word of the Ṛṣi is beyond reply. Blessed One, what now is the appropriate time for the prince and Kuraṅgī? The marriage must be commenced first.
Nārada: But the Gāndharva marriage was already completed at its own proper time.
Kuntibhoja: I desire that it be witnessed by the sacred fire.

Nārada: [He is] always like one who has fire as his witness. Nevertheless, for the sake of pleasing your own people, have the prince brought here quickly along with his wife, after having him perform the rites merely through a domestic priest.
Kuntibhoja: Holy sir! Here I go.
Nārada: Stay, sir. Bhūtika! You go.
Bhūtika: As the Blessed One commands. (Exit.
Kuntibhoja: Blessed One, I have something to report.
Nārada: Come this way; speak freely.

Kuntibhoja: "O Blessed One, I previously brought Kuraṅgī with the intention of giving her to Jayavarman, the son of Sudarśanā; thus she already has a protector. Tell me, what should be done now? Nārada: "I shall do so. Stay in a secluded place for a moment.
Kuntibhoja: "So be it. (He does so.)
Nārada: Sudarśanā! Come this way. Sudarśanā: Venerable sir! Here I am.
Nārada: Have you not heard my words?
Sudarśanā: I have heard the praise of the virtues of the prince of Sauvīra. Nārada: Do not say so! You have forgotten that your eldest son was born from the god Agni.
Sudarśanā: Ah, even this the Blessed One knows.
Nārada: "Just follow my command for now. Sudarśanā: "I shall do so. Let the Blessed One speak. (I shall do so. Let the Blessed One speak.
Nārada: "This son of yours was born from Agni. At the very moment of the birth of your sister Sūcetanā, her own son departed for heaven. This son of yours has been given by you to your sister."

The King of Sauvīra, being content with what was within his reach, performed acts befitting his joy and gave him the name Viṣṇusena. Because this youth, who possessed superhuman form, strength, vigor, and prowess, had slain the Asura Avirūpadhārin as he grew in power, the people called Viṣṇusena "Avimāraka" (the Slayer of Avimāraka). Then, having fallen due to a Brahmin’s curse, he beheld Kuraṅgī on the day of the elephant-panic; his desire having arisen, he united with her through great manly effort. While he was being examined by the guards of the maidens’ quarters—who were suspicious of Kuraṅgī’s presence—he was [consumed] by fire.

He went out, having been concealed by the Blessed One. Out of world-weariness, he entered the fire; however, as his father, the Blessed One, embraced him with love, the fire did not burn him. Thinking he would fall from the mountain, he climbed a certain peak.
Sudarśanā: Oh, what a calamity! (Aho accāhidaṃ!)

Nārada: There, a certain Vidyādhara, delighted merely by the sight of her form, affectionately gave me a single ring that grants invisibility; wearing it on the right finger, one becomes invisible, while with the left, one remains in one's natural state.
Sudarśanā: Wonderful, wonderful! (Astonishing, astonishing!)

Nārada: Then, holding it with his right finger, he entered the inner apartments of Kuṇtibhoja along with the Brahmin named Santuṣṭa as if they were his own home; there, sporting at will with Kuraṅgī, he dwells in happiness. This is the news. What should be done now?

Sudarśanā: Immediately after my noble lady was deceived, my heart has been as if set in motion; it yearns with curiosity. Blessed One! During these days, Kuraṅgī has been [the object of] King Jayavarman’s affection.
[She] asks: "From this day forward, she has become one to be honored by him. [Anantaramāryā]: "Deceived by the noble lady, my heart seems to tremble; yet it is gladdened by curiosity.

Blessed One, during these days, Kuraṅgī was asked whether she was the wife of Jayavarman. From today onwards, she has become one to be honored by him. Nārada: "What you have said is entirely consistent with noble lineage. But how can the eldest wife now be given to a younger man? Sudarśanā! Let it be told to Kāśirāja Jayavarman."
"Kuraṅgī is older [in age]," [he said]. "But surely there is one younger than Kuraṅgī named Sumitrā; she shall become the wife of Jayavarman.
Sudarśanā: "The word of the sage has been accepted. (The word of the sage has been accepted.
Nārada: "Go, follow Kuntibhoja."
Sudarśanā: "As the venerable one commands.
(Then enters Avimāraka, Kuraṅgī, and Bhūtika, dressed in bridal attire.
Avimāraka: "Oh! I am as if put to shame by this turn of events."
Having witnessed that confusion caused by the elephant at that time,
those who now proclaim my prowess—
have they truly understood this account?
They cast the blame for their own moral failings upon me. || 15 ||

(Walking around and looking) Ah, this is indeed the venerable Nārada! He is the one whose intellect is intent upon both curses and favors, whose throat is well-versed in the Vedas and songs, and who, having diligently instigated enmities among those who were once affectionate, brings peace to ruined affairs. (16)
Kuntibhoja: This way, this way, young man! Pay your respects to the celestial sage, the tutelary deity of your own lineage.
Avimāraka: Blessed one! I pay my respects.
Nārada: May it be well with you and your wife.
Avimāraka: I am favored! Uncle, I salute you. Kuntibhoja: Come, come, my child!
Conquer the foremost of Brahmins through patience; conquer those who seek refuge through compassion.
Conquer yourself through the realization of reality; conquer the kings with your splendor.
Avimāraka: I am favored.
Kuntibhoja: Child! This way, this way; salute your father. Avimāraka: O father! I salute you.
The King of Sauvīra: Come, come, my child!
Adorned with a most excellent and beautiful attire, your bright face mingled with the salutation of your elders;
like us, let your eyes be filled with tears of joy as you gaze here upon your own son.
"Son! Pay your respects to your maternal uncle.
Avimāraka: "Maternal uncle! I pay my respects. Kuntibhoja: "Come, come, my child!"
Be like Hari through auspicious deeds performed with constant application;
be like Daśaratha through truthful and firm words;
and be like a father through gifts constantly offered.
By his own self, which is well-subdued, and by his prowess. || 11 ||
The King of Sauvīra: My son, salute Sudarśanā.
Kuntibhoja: It seems improper to salute Sudarśanā without first saluting Sucetanā.
Nārada: There is a reason for this; let Sudarśanā be saluted.
Both: Let it be done so. Avimāraka: Lady! I salute you.
Sudarśanā: Son! Live long together with her. (Embracing him) It has been a long time since you were seen. Today, I have experienced the joy of attaining a son. (Son! Live long together with her.)
"You have been seen after a long time! Today I have experienced the joy of the fulfillment of my desire for a son. (She weeps.
Kuntibhoja: "But look at her, whose eyes are filled with curiosity and tears, and whose two breasts are overflowing with milk."
Without revealing that she has looked upon her mother,
my highly intelligent [daughter] assumes the very role of a nursemaid.
Nārada: Enough with excessive affection. Let Sucetanā and Sudarśanā enter the inner apartments of the maidens along with their wives and son.
Kuntibhoja: As the Blessed One commands.
Sudarśanā: As the Blessed One commands. (yad bhagavānājñāpayati.)
Nārada: Let the King of Sauvīra be dismissed at once to return to his own country. Let Sumitrā be given to Jayavarman, the King of Kāśi. You too remain present here.
Kuntibhoja: I am favored.
Nārada: O Kuntibhoja! What other pleasing service may I offer you?
Kuntibhoja said: "If the Blessed One is pleased with me, what more could I desire?
May there be constant welfare for cows and Brahmins, and may there be happiness for all creatures in the world."
Nārada: O King of Sauvīra, what further favor may I bestow upon you?
King of Sauvīra: If the Blessed One is pleased with me, what more could I possibly desire?
[I have already seen] this earth, which wears the dark-blue garment of the surging ocean—
May the lord of men rule over our earth. || 21 ||
(Bharata-vākya) May the cows be free from dust; may the enemy's army be pacified;
and may this entire earth be ruled by our lion among kings. 22.
(All exit) The Sixth Act.
